Friday, September 11, 2026

11:00 am Shaker Herb Garden Tour Enfield Shaker Museum Garden

All dates: Sep 11, Sep 18, Sep 25, Oct 2, Oct 9, Oct 16, Oct 23, Oct 30

Weekly Shaker Herb Garden Tour

with Herbalist Happy Griffiths

Fridays at 11 am, meet by the rose bushes in the garden

Join renowned herbalist and founder of the Enfield Shaker Museum Herb Garden, Happy Griffiths, for a guided tour through one of the Museum’s most beloved living exhibits.

Discover the fascinating history of the Shakers’ herb-growing traditions as you explore beds of culinary, medicinal, aromatic, and dye plants. Along the way, Happy will share stories of how these herbs were cultivated and used by the Enfield Shakers, as well as their practical uses in today’s gardens and homes.

With decades of experience as an herbalist, educator, and the visionary behind the Museum’s herb garden, Happy brings each tour to life with engaging insights and a deep appreciation for the connections between people, plants, and history. The Museum’s herb garden features many of the same plants that were grown by the Shakers as part of their thriving herb and medicine enterprise.

Fridays at 11:00 a.m.

Tours are free with Museum admission and are open to visitors of all ages. Whether you’re an avid gardener, curious about herbal traditions, or simply looking for a beautiful way to experience the Museum grounds, this tour offers a unique opportunity to explore the living legacy of the Enfield Shakers.

What to Expect

Tours last approximately one hour and take place rain or shine, except in the case of thunder or lightning. Much of the tour is outdoors in full sun, so we recommend dressing for the weather, wearing comfortable walking shoes, and bringing water, sunscreen, or rain gear as needed.

The herb garden features maintained paths, but visitors should expect some uneven terrain. Benches are available in both sunny and shaded areas throughout the garden for those who would like to sit during the tour.

Visitors are encouraged to engage all of their senses. You’ll have opportunities to see, smell, and ~when invited by your guide~ even taste selected herbs. To help preserve the garden and support the Museum’s educational mission, we ask that visitors do not pick plants or harvest herbs during the tour.

3 pm - 4 pm PhD Thesis Defense: Douglas Beahm academic Rm 232, Cummings Hall (Jackson Conf Rm)/ Online

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 981 1878 3645
Passcode: 219869

Abstract: A tremendous number of quantitative measurements have been made on biological cellular pathways, contributing to a massive body of knowledge about how living things work. Yet, we are scarcely able to quantitatively predict the behavior of whole biological cellular systems from the measures of their constituent molecular parts and cell populations. Furthermore, current technologies cannot directly measure many biological quantities of interest. To aid in addressing these gaps, we contribute dynamical models of cellular pathways as analog electrical circuits – suitable for analog and probabilistic computing in digitally programmable chips. They may also be represented and simulated in deterministic and stochastic ordinary differential equations (ODEs) on traditional digital computers. Specifically, we develop a model of SARS-CoV-2 infection that fits biological data; explains the effects of age, sex, viral variant, and treatment type on infection dynamics; and enables drug cocktail formulation via circuit design. Then, we present six fundamental behaviors of immune-pathogen feedback circuits that emerge as we vary immune vs. pathogen parameters in a parameter-outcome phase plane plot. We demonstrate an application of Dijkstra’s path-finding algorithm that selects optimal dose amounts, dose schedules, and drug cocktails for treatment regimen design. The algorithm helps place us in the “cure outcome” region of our prior phase plane plots. ATP/energy metabolism is known to be important in cellular stochastics and antibiotic persistence. We create an analog circuit model of E. coli ATP metabolism that fits experimental data to infer ATP production and consumption rates across growth stages. We also fit a novel model of antibiotic persister cell dynamics to biphasic killing curve data from antibiotic-treated E. coli cultures in order to measure the antibiotic-induced persister formation rate. Our work demonstrates the many ways in which analog electrical circuit models can be beneficially used to predict, analyze, design, simulate, and repair biological systems.

Thesis Committee: Rahul Sarpeshkar (chair), Margaret Ackerman, Daniel Schultz, Edward Stites (Yale University)

6:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution Hill Library 1151 Parker Mtn Rd STRAFFORD NH 03884

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

"Mary was well prepared and is a wonderful educator and speaker. She knows her subject well and her enthusiasm was evident. The slides and stories she chose were perfect for the subject and we could tell she knows a lot more than she could cram into the presentation. Mary is a valuable resource for learning NH history."

- Previous HTG host

6:00pm Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England Milton Town hall 55 Industrial Drive Milton NH 03851

Through architecture unique to northern New England, this illustrated talk focuses on several case studies that show how farmers converted their typical separate house and barns into connected farmsteads. Thomas Hubka's research in his award-winning book, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England, demonstrates that average farmers were, in fact, motivated by competition with farmers in other regions of America, who had better soils and growing seasons and fewer rocks to clear. The connected farmstead organization, housing equal parts mixed-farming and home-industry, was one of the collective responses to the competitive threat. 

Handicap accessable and free to the public.

Humanities to GoThomas HubkaMilton NH Historical societySandra Woods, 603.652.8735

Aug 6 – Sep 12, 2026 Converse with the Crossroads of the Wind Main Gallery- AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Converse with the Crossroads of the Wind Brings Together Six Artists Exploring Resilience, Transformation, and the Natural World

Clifford B. West Gallery and Rebecca Lawrence Gallery Entry

Six artists — Cheryl Betz, Thia Daniels, Marisa Green, Patty Hudak, Carla Kimball, and Anna Prikazchikova — are featured in Converse with the Crossroads of the Wind, a group exhibition examining what it means to remain present and rooted at the intersection of forces beyond our control. The wind does not ask permission before it changes direction. It arrives, shifts the landscape, and moves on, leaving behind evidence of its passing in bent branches, scattered seeds, and the long memory of those who stood in its path.

Cheryl Betz enters the conversation with urgency. Her paintings, begun during a residency at the Vermont Studio Center following the November 2024 election, bear the marks of rapid transformation — both personal and political. The surfaces are dense and heavily worked: layers of dark ground buried under collaged mulberry paper, Chinese text, ash, and acrylic that drips and bleeds as though the canvas cannot hold what has been pressed into it. Bamboo stalks rise in acid yellow through deep crimson and shadow, while cartoony animal forms lurk half-submerged, signifiers of greed, anger, and ignorance made strange by the beauty surrounding them. In the large lotus painting, three luminous blossoms float above darkness containing figures ancient as temple carvings, while wire roots spill from the canvas's lower edge down the wall. Betz holds corruption and resilience in the same frame until they become inseparable, the light genuinely dependent on the dark beneath it.

Thia Daniels is drawn to what cannot be named. The liminal — that in-between, undefinable threshold — recurs throughout her paintings like an uninvited guest who turns out to be necessary. In Daniels' hands, the uncertain is not something to be corrected but something to be inhabited with joy.

Marisa Green approaches the crossroads through cycles of loss and return. Her room-sized installation Samsara/Samara fills the gallery with thousands of suspended maple seeds cascading from wooden rods overhead, transitioning from living green to the amber and rust of autumn before releasing into a gathered pile on the floor. The piece enacts what it names: the Sanskrit samsara, the endless cycle of death and rebirth, made visible in a single breath held across an entire room. Nature, in Green's vision, is quietly instructive — most legible when mortality draws close and the heart finally opens to teachings it might otherwise miss.

Patty Hudak works across scales and surfaces, bringing together intimate mokuhanga prints and a vast acrylic-on-voile painting. There, Through the Broken Branches, Go is overwhelming in the best sense: sheer fabric painted in deep teals, aquas, and glacial whites, hung so that light passes through it, transforming a forest interior into something simultaneously shelter and exposure. Whether intimate or monumental, Hudak's work channels memories of moving through nature into structures of line and pattern, holding transformation and unseen presences in forms that feel both ancient and urgently present.

Carla Kimball began as a photographer of ordinary beauty, attuned to stillness. Her four short-form videos mark a deliberate pivot toward motion — toward the flows and fluctuations of the natural world that static images cannot fully hold — asking viewers to remember what it feels like to be genuinely connected to the world outside the screen.

Anna Prikazchikova works in paper, flat sheets transformed through cut and layer into landscapes of form and shadow, where negative space becomes as active as what surrounds it. Her intricate papercuts invite viewers to slow down, wander, and find their own meaning within winding forms.

Together, these six artists do not offer a single answer to the moment we find ourselves in. What they offer is harder and more necessary. Betz buries light under ash and still it surfaces. Green fills a room with falling seeds and calls it a guardian. Hudak paints a forest on sheer fabric and lets the light pass through. Daniels finds joy in what cannot be held. Kimball turns the camera toward a world changing faster than we can witness it. Prikazchikova cuts through paper until shadow becomes meaning. Across every surface and scale — paint and voile, seed and wire, paper and light — these artists practice the same insistence: that to make something beautiful in difficult times is not escape but resistance, not a turning away but a turning toward.

The wind shifts. The crossroads remains. The conversation continues.

Aug 6 – Sep 12, 2026 Steve Arcone and Talia Roberts Main Gallery- AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

A dual exhibition pairing the work of two artists whose practices, though rooted in different mediums and geographies, converge in a shared devotion to the slow, patient observation of the natural world.

Steve Arcone | Icescapes in the Abstract: Images from New Hampshire Ponds

In Icescapes in the Abstract, photographer Steve Arcone turns his macro lens on the small, overlooked worlds that form and dissolve across the surfaces of New Hampshire ponds during the shoulder seasons — late fall, mid-winter, and early spring. Working from 2021 to 2026, Arcone documented the fleeting architectures produced by cycles of daytime thaw and nighttime freezing: star-like crystal growths radiating from host twigs and branches, ladder-like mosaics born of repetitive crystallographic twinning, melt pools coexisting with intact ice, and fractures both curved and complex.

Shot at scales ranging from 8 to 40 centimeters in width, the resulting images are at once scientifically precise and thoroughly abstract. Macro imaging lenses collapse depth, rendering each subject as a near-flat field of texture and pattern — not unlike the picture plane of a painting. Organic debris — leaf species, pine needles, pinecones, lichen, wood — occasionally grounds the viewer in context, but these clues are easily overridden by the strangeness and beauty of what surrounds them.

Arcone, who bridges the worlds of science and art, invites viewers not to identify but to look. Many titles draw from classical or jazz compositions, yet he encourages visitors to linger and offer their own interpretations. The moods he seeks to impart — inquisitiveness, serenity, amazement — are the moods of genuine encounter with the unfamiliar.

Talia Roberts | Earth Memories, Moon Visions

Painter Talia Roberts works from the ground up — literally. For this series, Roberts collected rock samples from Vermont's Green Mountains, processing them by hand into pigments using a mortar and pestle, then mulling each pigment with walnut oil to produce a range of non-synthetic oil paints. The resulting palette carries the particular gravity of place: these are not colors chosen from a manufacturer's chart but colors extracted from the land itself.

Earth Memories, Moon Visions presents these pigments in paintings organized around a recurring circular motif — an image of the moon that doubles as a meditation on time, geology, and duality. The works are presented in pairs, placing opposites in productive tension: earth and sky, light and dark, memory and vision, representation and abstraction. Together they suggest that the landscape and the cosmos are not separate realms but continuous ones, each reflected in the other.

Roberts describes her practice as a counterpoint to the visual saturation of contemporary life. By emphasizing materiality and process — the stone become pigment, the pigment become paint, the paint become image — she asks viewers to slow down, to attend more closely, to notice what is quiet and subtle. The series is, finally, a tribute to the Earth itself: the place that holds us.

A Conversation Between Two Practices

The pairing of these two exhibitions is not incidental. Arcone and Roberts arrive at their subjects by different means — one through the optical precision of a camera, the other through the physical labor of pigment-making — but they share a fundamental orientation: both are artists who go to the natural world with patience, who find their images through sustained attention rather than imposition.

Both bodies of work are deeply rooted in the landscapes of northern New England, and both negotiate the boundary between representation and abstraction. Arcone's ice formations resist easy identification; Roberts's painted circles slip between the literal and the cosmic. In each case, the familiar is rendered strange, and the strange is rendered beautiful. There is also, in both practices, an ethics of looking. Arcone's macro scale makes visible what passes unnoticed underfoot; Roberts's slow extraction of pigment from stone insists on the intelligence and meaning held in the material world. Placed in dialogue, these exhibitions become a meditation on scale — the intimate and the infinite, the microscopic and the geological — and on how attentive looking can bridge them.

Saturday, September 12, 2026

9:00 am Hike Into History: Feast Grounds Enfield Shaker Museum

Free – $15

Hike Into History

Saturday September 12th at 9:00am

Meet at the Stone Machine Shop across the street from the Enfield Shaker Museum

Free With Museum Admission

Want to explore the Shaker trails while learning about the history of the buildings and structures along the way? Then join us for our monthly Hike into History!
The Shakers of the 1800s would travel up twice a year to their Feast Grounds for worship. On this guided hike, learn why the Shakers started worshiping outside, what they did at the Feast Grounds, and why they stopped? Our Education Coordinator will lead the hike to the Feast Grounds, answering these questions, and point out spots of interest including the morning view of Lake Mascoma. This month’s hike will be a 1.15 mile out-and-back style hike and will happen in the rain or shine. If there is thunder, the hike will be cancelled.
This hike will be outside and in the woods. Please come prepared with water, appropriate footwear and layers, and be prepared for sun, rain, bugs, and ticks.

PARKING INFORMATION: Parking can be found at the Enfield Shaker Museum or directly at the Stone Machine Shop. Please note if you park at the Museum, you will have to cross Route 4A and there is no crosswalk

ACCESSIBILITY: This 1.15 mile out-and-back style hike will have about 260ft of elevation change and can get a little steep in some places. The trail is wide, has divots from washouts, roots, and rocks, and has multiple sections of walking around tall grass

All funds go towards furthering the Education Mission of the Enfield Shaker Museum

10:00am Duck Race Auburn Village 0

Thousands gather each September for a fun-filled family event hosted by the Auburn Historical Association. The Duck Race is the main attraction with prizes for the 10 fastest ducks, including a top prize of $1,000! There will be food trucks, local artisans and authors, a small petting farm, an apple pie contest, a kids baking contest, music and climbing wall. Active demonstrations of wool spinning and carding, cider pressing, blacksmithing, rug braiding, pottery making and so much more are ongoing continuously during the day. 12:00 pm Shaker Herb Garden Tour Enfield Shaker Museum Garden

All dates: Sep 12, Sep 19, Sep 26, Oct 3, Oct 10, Oct 17, Oct 24, Oct 31

Weekly Shaker Herb Garden Tour

with Museum Interpreter Lisa Torres

Saturdays at Noon, meet by the Great Stone Dwelling, outside the Gift Shop Entrance

Join Museum Interpreter Lisa Torres for a guided tour through the Enfield Shaker Museum Herb Garden, one of the Museum’s most beloved living exhibits.

Discover the fascinating history of the Shakers’ herb-growing traditions as you explore beds of culinary, medicinal, aromatic, and dye plants. Along the way, Lisa will share stories of how these herbs were cultivated and used by the Enfield Shakers, while exploring the ecology, botany, and practical uses of the plants growing in the garden today.

A lifelong science educator with a background in environmental chemistry and ecology, Lisa brings curiosity, enthusiasm, and a love of learning to every tour. After a 31-year career teaching science at Lebanon High School, she joined the Museum as an Interpreter and educator, where she enjoys helping visitors discover the rich connections between plants, history, and the Shaker way of life.

The Museum’s herb garden features many of the same plants that were grown by the Shakers as part of their thriving herb and medicine enterprise.

Saturdays at Noon.

Tours are free with Museum admission and are open to visitors of all ages. Whether you’re an avid gardener, curious about herbal traditions, or simply looking for a beautiful way to experience the Museum grounds, this tour offers a unique opportunity to explore the living legacy of the Enfield Shakers.

What to Expect

Tours last approximately one hour and take place rain or shine, except in the case of thunder or lightning. Much of the tour is outdoors in full sun, so we recommend dressing for the weather, wearing comfortable walking shoes, and bringing water, sunscreen, or rain gear as needed.

The herb garden features maintained paths, but visitors should expect some uneven terrain. Benches are available in both sunny and shaded areas throughout the garden for those who would like to sit during the tour.

Visitors are encouraged to engage all of their senses. You’ll have opportunities to see, smell, and ~when invited by your guide~ even taste selected herbs. To help preserve the garden and support the Museum’s educational mission, we ask that visitors do not pick plants or harvest herbs during the tour.

Sep 12 Sep 19 Sep 26 Oct 3 Oct 10 Oct 17 Oct 24 Oct 31
1:00pm Late in Arriving, How Electricity Changed Rural New Hampshire Life East Grafton Union Church 80 Turnpike Rd Grafton NH 03240

Imagine a New Hampshire town where some people enjoyed the benefits of electricity – lighting at the flick of a switch and reliable heating controlled by a thermostat – while others lived with smelly kerosene lamps and smoky box stoves. In New Hampshire, during the first half of the 20th century,  residents of developed communities enjoyed the transformative benefits of electric power while those in the sparsely populated regions lived and worked in conditions little changed from the 19th century.  

It took the coming of the New Deal's Rural Electrification Administration and a determined band of farmers to overcome opposition from the established private utilities to create the New Hampshire Electric Cooperative in 1939. Despite labor and material shortages during World War II, within a decade, power came to almost all of the previously unserved areas of the state. For thousands of households, this meant relief from the drudgery of the wood-fueled cookstove, the washboard and the kerosene lamp. Reliable electric power similarly brought new ways of life to farmers and artisans. This program will explore how these developments changed civic and social life in New Hampshire’s countryside, and touch the ways the disparity of broadband access in the state today echoes these earlier struggles.

For handicap access, there is a ramp on the down-hill side of the building towards the back.

Also known as Provincetown Prints, white line woodcuts are a distinctive technique of multicolored prints cut from a single block of wood. Small grooves between the elements of a design create the white lines in the image. This process uses watercolor paints and can be done without a press.

All materials included in price.

2 Sessions, Sept 12-13 | 10 AM-4 PM

Marilyn Syme has decades of experience as a painter and printmaker and is passionate about this artform. Syme began studying white line woodblock printing, also called “Provincetown Print” because it was developed by a group of Provincetown and Cape Cod printmakers in 1915, under Kathryn Smith of Provincetown. An accomplished artist, Syme has also studied woodcuts in Tuscany, Italy, and solar printing in recent years.

Organ Recital

NH Chapter of American Guild of Organists

Members of the New Hampshire chapter of the American Guild of Organists will be featured in the final concert of the 2026 season. Five organists will perform works that display the organ’s capacity and breadth of color. The program will include Hungarian Rhapsodies, The Bells of St Anne de Beaupre by Alexander Russell, Pachelbel Toccata in E minor, Trumpet Tune by Nicholas Bowden, compositions by Gerald Near, Thomas Crawford, Brenda Portman, J. S. Bach, and More.

Organ Restoration Update

Bob Waters and Richard Nickerson are continuing to address important restoration needs on the Casavant organ in the Museum’s Mary Keane Chapel. This fall and winter they removed and completely rebuilt the wind chest that receives and regulates the air pressure produced by the organ’s electric blower. This included replacing all the original leather work that controls the release of air to the organ pipes. In addition to maintaining the organ’s tuning, they have been repairing coupling mechanisms that have failed. Unfortunately the Casavant company no longer makes certain replacement parts, so some aspects of the restoration work requires creative problem solving. We are fortunate to have two craftsmen, well versed in the intricacies of Casavant organ construction, caring for this precious instrument.

Thank you for your support of their ongoing restoration work.

6 pm - 9 pm Spectral Dome Room,Shattuck Observatory, 15 Observatory Rd, Hanover, NH 03755

SPECTRAL is a 4+1 channel spatial sound installation built from real measurement data recorded by instruments aboard NASA's Parker Solar Probe (PSP). The work translates humanity's closest-ever machine perception of the Sun into an immersive, physically grounded sonic experience.

As the fastest human-made object ever built and the one to travel closest to the Sun, PSP moves through the outermost layer of the solar atmosphere, the corona, within an extreme radiation environment, withstanding a surrounding plasma that reaches temperatures in the millions of degrees Celsius. Its scientific instruments act like antennae reaching toward the Sun, recording electromagnetic field fluctuations, plasma properties, and energetic particle activity invisible to the human eye.

In this work, PSP is cast as the sole perceiving subject, its first-person perspective anchoring the piece. Four historic milestones from its journey form the work's movements: its first perihelion pass, its first crossing of the Alfvén Surface into the corona, its passage through a violent solar storm, and its record-breaking closest approach. These four data segments form the work's four chapters, interweaving raw physical waveforms with fragmented, granular textures to reconstruct a deep-space auditory narrative traversing invisible magnetic fields and solar storms.

SPECTRAL is created by Yuening Cai (MSDA, Department of Computer Science), with scientific collaboration from Luke Kathmann (PhD student, Department of Physics and Astronomy). The project is supported by the Arts Integration Initiative Grant, awarded by the Hopkins Center for the Arts.

On his fourth and final trip to the United States in 1824-1825, Americans in all 24 states welcomed Lafayette with unbridled admiration, gratitude, and love. In this talk, Hoffman will set the scene for the Farewell Tour and explore the causes of Lafayette’s rock star reception.

Sep 15 Sep 22 Sep 29 Oct 6
10 am - 11 am MS Thesis Defense: Kavi Krsnadas academic Rm 035, ECSC

Abstract: Inverters for residential power systems in North America often rely on line-frequency neutral-forming autotransformers to create a split-phase power configuration from a single-phase inverter output. Particularly with bidirectional electric vehicle systems, off-board neutral formation is required. Autotransformers used in these applications are based on century-old technology that suffers from poor light load efficiency and high mass. A single-stage solid-state autotransformer alternative is proposed to reduce size and standby loss compared to the line-frequency counterpart. The proposed converter builds on the 2:1 switched capacitor topology, most notably with the inclusion of bidirectional voltage blocking switches. Implications of ac-ac operation for this well-described dc-dc topology are discussed, including bidirectional switch operation and approximate loss modeling. A prototype has been designed and tested for proof-of-concept, leveraging newly available monolithic bidirectional GaN switches. The 4 kW, 240 Vac to split-phase 120 Vac prototype achieves a peak efficiency of 98.9% and power density of 7.18 kW/kg with resistive loads, using fixed timing to achieve partial zero voltage switching throughout the line cycle. A demonstration of 1 kVA operation with a nonlinear reactive load is also shown. The solid-state autotransformer prototype has 3.45x lower no-load loss and 16x smaller mass than a line-frequency autotransformer with a comparable power rating.

Thesis Committee: (Chair) Charles R. Sullivan, Jason T. Stauth, Cong Chen

12 pm - 1 pm DCC Grand Rounds with Amber E. Barnato, MD, MPH, MS DHMC, Auditorium E

Amber E. Barnato, MD, MPH, MS is the John E. Wennberg Distinguished Professor and Chair of Health Policy & Clinical Practice and the Director, The Dartmouth Institute for Health Policy and Clinical Practice. Dr. Barnato is a physician-scientist trained in public health and preventive medicine, health policy research, and hospice and palliative medicine. A practicing palliative care physician, Dr. Barnato’s research focuses on understanding the causes and consequences of variation in end-of-life intensive care unit (ICU) and life-sustaining treatment use among seriously ill older adults. She uses an array of scientific methods, including claims data analysis, participant observation and interviewing, high-fidelity simulation experiments, and randomized behavioral trials. Her work increasingly focuses on the interplay between organizational norms, provider-patient communication, and implicit cognition, and how these phenomena produce racial disparities in end-of-life treatment. Dr. Barnato has been continuously funded by the National Institutes of Health since 2003, has been the Principal Investigator or Project Leader of more than 25 extramurally funded awards, authored more than 190 peer-reviewed publications, and mentored more than 70 pre-doctoral and post-doctoral scientists. Her academic program development work focuses on early career development for clinician-scientists, including establishing and directing the Clinical Scientist Training Program at the University of Pittsburgh and founding the Dartmouth Health Equity Research Pathways Program at Dartmouth. As part of her public advocacy work, Dr. Barnato oversees the Dartmouth Atlas of Health Care and collects and shares stories from diverse family members regarding their experiences making life-support decisions for patients in the ICU at the website www.ICUStoryWeb.org. Her newest curiosity is how psychedelic assisted therapy could change the paradigm of medical practice, both by offering novel pathways for treating mental health conditions and existential distress associated with life-threatening illness, and by ameliorating the trauma the health care delivery system on clinicians, thereby increasing their capacity for compassion, empathy, and trust in their patients’ capacity for self-healing.

12:00pm Uprooted: Heartache and Hope in New Hampshire YMCA of Concord 15 North State Street Concord NH 03301

Uprooted is a 30-minute documentary based on interviews collected during New Hampshire Humanities' Fences & Neighbors initiative on immigration. It tells the story of five refugees who escaped from war-torn countries to resettle in New Hampshire. The film explores what it means to be a refugee and how it feels to make a new life in a strange place, often without English language skills, family, a job, or community contacts. The film leaves us pondering questions of belonging and citizenship. What does it mean to be an American? Once a refugee, are you destined always to be a refugee? What are our responsibilities toward one another? A New Hampshire Humanities presenter introduces the film and leads a post-film discussion.

 

The Concord YMCA is located in downtown Concord. The event will have a ramp or elevator access. There is city parking in the State Street parking garage.

There will be light refreshments served.

2 pm - 3 pm Physics and Astronomy Condensed Matter Seminar- Dr. Benjamin Levitan, Sherbrooke academic Wilder 111 and Zoom

Abstract: Every mean-field superconductor has a complex order parameter, giving rise to two collective modes corresponding to amplitude (“Schmid-Higgs”) and phase (“Anderson-Bogoliubov-Goldstone”) fluctuations. Superconductors with additional structure can host a richer variety of collective modes, in the form of fluctuations which explore the larger order-parameter configuration space. Examples include Leggett modes (given multiple bands), Bardasis-Schrieffer modes (given one or more subdominant pairing channels), and clapping modes (given a multicomponent pairing channel). Crystal symmetries often impose selection rules which keep these modes dark in linear optical response. In this talk, I will outline a general effective-action approach to the theory of superconducting collective modes and describe how explicit or spontaneous symmetry breaking can optically activate them. I will show how emerging two-dimensional superconductors offer a promising platform for the study of exotic collective excitations, with special attention to rhombohedral graphene multilayers, where gate-tunable out-of-plane displacement fields or valley polarization can provide the requisite symmetry breaking.

Hosted By: Assistant Professor Rufus Boyack 

Zoom Link: https://dartmouth.zoom.us/j/99960465228?

3:30 pm - 5:00 pm The American Revolution and the Fate of the World Online - Zoom
When we think of the American Revolution, we picture 13 colonies squaring off against the British Crown in a spirited bid for independence. But this version of the story is only half the truth—and perhaps not even the most interesting half. In this riveting program, historian and author Richard Bell invites us to rediscover the Revolution as a world war that unleashed chaos, opportunity, and transformation across six continents—from the sugar fields of the Caribbean to the court of the King of Mysore, from refugee camps on the Canadian frontier to political uprisings in Sierra Leone and Peru—and traces the far-flung reverberations of the war through the lives of the people it displaced, empowered, or destroyed. Richard Bell is Professor of History at the University of Maryland and author of the book Stolen: Five Free Boys Kidnapped into Slavery and their Astonishing Odyssey Home which was a finalist for the George Washington Prize and the Harriet Tubman Prize. He has held major research fellowships at Yale, Cambridge, and the Library of Congress and is the recipient of the National Endowment of the Humanities Public Scholar award and the Andrew Carnegie Fellowship. His new book, The American Revolution and the Fate of the World, was published by Penguin in November 2025.

He maintains a list of upcoming events at Richard-Bell.com. Cost:Osher Members: $10

7:00pm Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England Alstead Town Hall (rear of fire statiom 9 Main Street Alstead NH 03602

Through architecture unique to northern New England, this illustrated talk focuses on several case studies that show how farmers converted their typical separate house and barns into connected farmsteads. Thomas Hubka's research in his award-winning book, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England, demonstrates that average farmers were, in fact, motivated by competition with farmers in other regions of America, who had better soils and growing seasons and fewer rocks to clear. The connected farmstead organization, housing equal parts mixed-farming and home-industry, was one of the collective responses to the competitive threat. 

The Town Hall is located at the rear of the fire station building. Limited parking is available near the entrance door. Additional parking is available on Main Street.

7:00pm Historic Lighthouses and Keepers of New Hampshire & Southern Maine Madbury Town Hall 13 Town Hall Road Madbury NH 03823

Jeremy D'Entremont highlights the fascinating stories of the lighthouse keepers and their families who, beginning in 1771, mainainted the lighthouses between Portsmouth, New Hampshire, and York, Maine: Portsmouth Harbor Light, Whaleback Light, White Island (Isles of Shoals) Light, Boon Island Light, and Cape Neddick "Nubble" Light. The histories of these lighthouses and their keepers reveal rich human interest stories and fascinating lore, from rescues and heroism to isolation and tragedy, and even ghost stories. The program also explores ongoing efforts to preserve these iconic maritime sentinels today.

7:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution Alton Public Library 100 Main Street ALTON NH 03809

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

"Mary was well prepared and is a wonderful educator and speaker. She knows her subject well and her enthusiasm was evident. The slides and stories she chose were perfect for the subject and we could tell she knows a lot more than she could cram into the presentation. Mary is a valuable resource for learning NH history."

- Previous HTG host

Onsite parking available and meeting room is at parking area level.

2:00pm US@250: Big Watch Bedford Public Library 3 Meetinghouse Road Bedford NH 03110


Be a part of something BIG: Join US@250: Big Watch, a statewide series of community-driven programs that bring Granite Staters together to watch, discuss, and reflect on the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence and American Revolution.

 

Join us to commemorate and reflect upon the 250th anniversary with a film screening and discussion. Together, we’ll watch a short (30 min) excerpt from THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION, a new film directed by Ken Burns, Sarah Botstein, and David Schmidt, followed by a community discussion. The featured segment from THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION,“The Spirit of Service,” explores service as a core American value, from the nation’s founding through to the present day – examining volunteerism, civic participation, public leadership, and more.


Expert facilitator Mohamed Defaa will guide thoughtful conversations about “remembering together,” considering questions such as:

    • What moments from our past define who we are and point to a shared future? 
    • What are the key historical moments in your town’s or community’s history? 
    • How does focusing on these moments shape your sense of your community’s future?

 

This program will last approximately 1.5 hours (30 minutes for film screening, 1 hour for facilitated discussion). Please make sure you have appropriate technology for the film screening, including a strong internet connection, large screen, and sound system. Please contact programs@nhhumanities.org for the link to the themed excerpt. 

Big Watch programs are made possible by a partnership between New Hampshire Humanities and New Hampshire PBS.

5:30pm Portraits of a Revolution Old Webster Courthouse/Plymouth Historical Society Museum Court Street Plymouth NH 03264

This program explores American portraits painted and sculpted during the years leading up to, and the decades after, the Revolution. The ideals, values and virtues expressly stated in our founding documents are easily identifiable in these portraits once we know how to “read” them. We will examine portraits of founding “fathers” and “mothers,” as well as of lesser-known individuals, as documents that can be read like texts. We will also discuss the tradition of portraiture, and the influences of earlier art movements, artists, and artifacts, that inform these American portraits. Audiences will be introduced to, and practice, some skills of art analysis and learn how art works can reveal so much about a culture.

5:30pm African American Soldiers and Sailors of New Hampshire During the American Revolution Portsmouth Athenaeum 9 Market Square Portsmouth NH 03801

One of the most interesting aspects of the American Revolution is the role played by African Americans in the fight for independence. Both free African Americans and those that were enslaved were key in manning state militias and Continental Army units, as well as serving on the high seas in the Navy and on privately armed ships. Indeed, their service to the colonies was crucial in a conflict that lasted nearly seven years. Prohibited from serving in military units and largely considered "undesirable elements," how is it that these African-American soldiers came to fight for the cause of liberty, even when their own personal liberty was not guaranteed?

Glenn Knoblock examines the history of African-American soldiers' service during the war, including how and why they enlisted, their interaction with white soldiers, service on the battlefields, how they were perceived by the enemy and the officers under whom they served, and their treatment after the war.

The First Amendment protects our most basic freedoms, none more important than freedom of speech. But what do we do about speech that threatens to destroy the social fabric? This presentation considers the constitutional arguments for and against hate speech codes and why the Supreme Court ruled against St. Paul's hate speech ordinance. If hate speech codes are unconstitutional, it falls on citizens to find other ways to counter hateful speech. We'll explore what capacities citizens need to preserve freedom and the social fabric. Could it be that persuasion and deliberation might be better strategies for all of us?

7 pm - 9 pm Wild Horse Nine (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell and Steve Buscemi star in Martin McDonagh's dark buddy comedy about CIA agents entangling with local Chilean students ahead of the 1973 coup.

Chile, 1973: after Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell), two veteran CIA operatives, wrap up a subversive undercover mission—destabilizing the democratically elected Allende and prepping his opponents for a military coup—they head to Easter Island on a mission, where Chris hopes to write his memoir. An encounter with two students (Mariana di Girolamo and Ailín Salas) hastens the erosion of their trust. 

Chris and Lee's back-and-forth banter—a mix of nostalgic camaraderie and acerbic oneupmanship brilliantly performed by Malkovich and Rockwell—makes Martin McDonagh's film a satirically funny buddy film for the ages, rivaling his own The Banshees of Inisherin. But McDonagh never shies from his clear-eyed and caustic view of the tragic consequences of America's cynical, destructive interventions abroad: This is a comedy with blood on its hands. Parker Posey, Steve Buscemi and Tom Waits provide dazzling support.

Special Passholder and Student-only screening

Sep 16 – Nov 14, 2026 a place visited only in dreams Linda Roesch Visual Arts Gallery and Gallery 3, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Opening reception Friday, September 25, 5-7 PM. On view September 16-November 14 | The Linda Roesch Visual Arts Gallery and Gallery 3

A Place Visited Only in Dreams brings together 35 artists who are each interested in exploring the shifting terrain of the subconscious, where logic dissolves and imagination reigns. Rooted in the legacy of Surrealism, this exhibition is composed of works that construct alternate realities—worlds shaped by dream imagery, memory fragments, intuition, and the irrational. Here, narratives unfold beyond the boundaries of waking life, where objects may float, figures transform, scale collapses, and time behaves unpredictably.

Surrealism has long offered a visual language for expressing what cannot be spoken directly: desire, fear, wonder, longing, and the strange poetry of the mind at rest. In this exhibition, you'll find artworks that embrace unexpected juxtapositions, uncanny atmospheres, and illogical pairings that provoke both unease and fascination. Whether playful or haunting, meditative or disruptive, these works invite viewers to step into spaces that feel familiar yet impossible— places visited only in dreams.

Step beyond waking reality. Enter the dream.

Exhibiting artists: Amy Abeyta, Jenna Marie Alderiso, Lucas Barrett, Kalli Bechtold, Fiorella Buck, Annabelle Cone, Annemarie Curlin, Elizabeth D'Amico, Thia Daniels, Samantha Eckert, Richard Fedorchak, Stephanie Gordon, Laura Graveline, Matthew Greenway, Naomi Hartov, Bruce Hasse, Marria Khan, Ed Kimball, Stephany Komen Hasse, Maggie mayfly Kundtz Joseph, Susan Maerlender, Emma Mehegan, Carl Mehrbach, Michaela Meyer, Jennifer Rickards, Lara Ronan, Kerin Rose, Cynthia Ross, Ann Saunderson, Tom Sennett, Nancy Sepe, Reinhart Sonnenburg, Richard Stamelman, Rio Del Sol Vasquez-Billin, Cathy Vincevic

Sep 17 Sep 24 Oct 1 Oct 8 Oct 15 Oct 22 Oct 29
9 am - 10 am MS Thesis Defense: Ryan Proulx academic Rm 232, Cummings Hall (Jackson Conf Rm)

Abstract: Countries such as the Central African Republic (CAR), South Sudan, and Somalia face cycles of conflict, political instability, low electrification rates, and the impacts of climate change. Renewable energy-driven electrification is often considered a key way to mitigate these challenges. However, designing and planning green electrification initiatives in fragile states requires complex decision-making involving multiple objectives and multiple stakeholders.

We implement a consensus-building framework and methodology to guide hybrid renewable energy system planning in fragile African states. Our study operationalizes an iterative approach to Majority Judgement (MJ) in planning energy systems for UN compounds and the surrounding local community. The case study structure mirrors a typical mini-grid (anchor client/community) demand profile.

We gather institutional data from 17 experts within the African energy transition from groups including the African Development Bank (AfDB), United Nations Department of Operational Support (UN DOS), and the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). The data are processed to produce three classes of inputs to the iterative approach to MJ : (1) direct stakeholder data, (2) stakeholder-data-influenced statistical best-fit utility functions, and (3) stakeholder-data-influenced LLM-derived utility functions. We compute the optimality gaps across all input classes in a 2-dimensional case (examining upfront cost and diesel consumption for mini-grid designs) and a 4-dimensional case (examining upfront cost, diesel consumption, community coverage, and system reliability for mini-grid designs). We find that low-diesel, high-community-coverage mini-grid designs with marginally reduced reliability provide the best compromise in the majority of cases across all input classes.

Thesis Committee: (Chair) Vikrant Vaze, Steve Peterson, Geoff Parker, Erin Mayfield, and Victoria Holt (Dickey Center for International Understanding)

12:15 pm - 1:45 pm Anthropology Colloquium w/ Dr. Jeffrey Hoelle, UC Santa Barbara academic · audience: Alumni, Faculty, Postdoc, Staff, Students-Graduate, Students-Undergraduate Haldeman 031

Anthropology Colloquium
Plants, Hair and the Aesthetic of Control in Frontier Amazonia
Jeffrey Hoelle, Professor of Anthropology
University of California, Santa Barbara

In this talk, Jeffrey Hoelle traces the imprint of cultivation across the naturally growing covers of the land and body—plants and hair. Drawing on ethnographic research in the Brazilian Amazon, Hoelle moves from the cattle pastures and agricultural fields at the edge of the rainforest to domestic lawns and hair salons in Brazilian cities and beyond. Hoelle explains how replacing tangled forests with geometric, "clean" pastures and everyday lawn care share a cultural logic with the ways that hair is managed, categorized, and judged in the city.  He argues that these seemingly disparate domains of agriculture, landscaping, and personal grooming are governed by a similar aesthetic of control. This unique pairing of land and body expands our understanding of cultivation as a practice and an ideological system that influences how we conceptualize the covers that grow on and around us, and challenges how we imagine our future relationship with the natural world.
 

Alumni, Faculty, Postdoc, Staff, Students-Graduate, Students-UndergraduateAnthropology Department

12:15 pm - 1:00 pm Artist Talk with Chris Sollars 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center

In his first solo exhibition at Dartmouth College, multidisciplinary artist and Associate Professor of Studio Art Chris Sollars presents The Neighbors, a new body of work inspired by coexistence and inquiry.

Set in rural Vermont, The Neighbors is a multimedia video installation about the non-human inhabitants of the lands around the artist’s home. After over two decades living in San Francisco, California, Sollars moved to Vermont in the fall of 2024. To get to know his new home and neighbors, he has spent the past two years interacting with his surroundings through slow listening and observation, learning them spatially and temporally.  This intentional gathering of information has taken the form of diaristic snapshots taken throughout the seasons, field recordings, the collection of discarded nests and materials, and the placement of wildlife cameras in the open woodland edges of his home, which neighbors a land trust, a national forest, and the Appalachian Trail.

Please join us for an Artist Talk at in the 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center, at 12:15 p.m. on Thursday, Sept. 17. 

The Neighbors is on view from Sept. 15 – Nov. 8, 2026.

12:15 pm - 1:15 pm HOOD SALON INFO SESSION Hood Museum of Art

Join exhibition curator Elizabeth Rice Mattison in Community and Exile: Artists in Paris, 1910–1939 to learn more about the upcoming Hood Salon! Coffee and snacks will be provided.

The exhibition features work from the Hood Museum’s collection by immigrant artists who sought refuge in Paris, from the beginning of the 20th century until World War II. Artists came to the city to escape persecution, societal strictures, and economic stagnation elsewhere in the world. Paris allowed them to build a community in their new home and to forge a thriving, interdisciplinary cultural scene.

In the same spirit of creative and cultural exchange, the museum is welcoming submissions from current Dartmouth graduate and undergraduate students of works that respond to or expand upon the themes and/or artworks in the exhibition. Selected works will be reproduced in a publication made available to gallery visitors within the exhibition. For more information about the Hood Salon, click here.

1:30pm Exemplary Country Estates of New Hampshire Scott-Farrar Community 11 Elm St Peterborough NH 03458

In the early 20th century, the New Hampshire Board of Agriculture launched a program to boost the rural economy and promote tourism through the sale of abandoned farms to summer residents. After introducing the country house movement, Cristina Ashjian focuses attention on some of the great country estates featured in the New Hampshire program between 1902 and 1913.

Which private estates were recognized as exemplary, and who were their owners? Using historic images and texts, Ashjian discusses well-known estates now open to the public such as The Fells on Lake Sunapee, The Rocks in Bethlehem, Saint-Gaudens National Historic Site in Cornish, and she includes local examples when possible.

Meet The Authors & Presenters

Elifgül Büyükoral was born and raised in Türkiye, where her close-knit family nurtured her love for books. Elifgül delved into the world of literature and language when she earned her BA in ESL. Fueled by her passion for storytelling, Elifgül moved to the United States to receive her MA in children’s literature from Simmons University. Elifgül writes stories that shine light on her heritage and Islamic faith, hoping to amplify diverse voices.

 

Evgenia Mantikas was born in Queens, raised on stories passed down for generations about villages on a faraway island in the Aegean. She is a middle-school teacher and holds a master’s degree in English literature from Fordham University and one in writing for children from Simmons University, where she met her coauthor. Evgenia’s work is a love letter to her culture and the village who raised her. When she isn't writing or teaching, Evgenia can be found talking about Percy Jackson, Taylor Swift, Avatar the Last Airbender, K-Dramas, and whales.        

 

Mary Nolin is the Connections program manager at New Hampshire Humanities and English as a Second Language Teacher at Second Start in Concord, NH. With over 10 years of international and domestic teaching experience, Mary is firm believer in the power of books to change lives. Mary has a Bachelor’s Degree in History and a Master’s in Education, both from the University of New Hampshire. However, her best education has come from her life experiences as a Peace Corps Volunteer, teacher, and mom.

7:00 pm - 8:45 pm Elsinore (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Andrew Scott and Olivia Colman star in this powerful true story of actor Ian Charleson preparing for the role of Hamlet at the National Theatre while seriously ill from AIDS.

"It's the greatest part you could ever play in the greatest theatre, and I'm jealous as fuck." In 1989, the actor Ian Charleson, whose role in Chariots of Fire brought celebrity (along with a certain notoriety among purist colleagues), is anxious to return to the stage. But the role of Hamlet at London's National Theatre eludes him. When the original actor suddenly quits, he receives his chance-of-a-lifetime opportunity. The double bind: he has AIDS, still a publicly taboo topic. 

The exquisite performance by Andrew Scott (All of Us Strangers) brings unforgettable insight and compassion to Charleson, and the story reflects the play's eternal themes: lies, secrets, subterfuge; love and friendships; being alive and facing death. Simon Stone's film, whose terrific cast includes Olivia Colman and Billie Piper, provides a timeless and resonant portrait of a man, in the throes of crisis, acting the best he can.

Get more info here.

8:00 am - 6:30 pm Boston Symphony Orchestra - A Day Trip Boston Symphony Hall, 301 Massachusetts Ave, Boston, MA 02115

Join Osher at Dartmouth for a world class musical day at the Boston Symphony Orchestra with Conductor Andris Nelsons and Pianist Emanuel Ax! The performance will feature Mozart's Piano Concerto No. 22, K.482 (1785) and Berlioz' Symphonie fantastique (1830).

Emanual Ax is known for his interpretations of Mozart's concertos, Piano Concerto No. 22 being the picture of elegance. Then Berlioz flips the mood entirely: his Symphonie fantastique (1830) was inspired by an artist's obsessive infatuation, his own execution, and a witches' sabbath, told purely through the orchestra.

We will travel to Boston, departing from Lebanon at 8:15 AM. We will arrive in Boston about two hours before the performance begins at 1:30 PM, leaving time for you to explore on your own! We will leave Boston immediately after the performance, returning to Lebanon around 6:30 PM.

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm Raising the Bar for Energy Storage R&D Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 937 4316 0035
Passcode: 411385

The US Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Electricity’s (OE) energy storage research, development, and demonstration (RD&D) portfolio accelerates innovation to deliver a reliable, secure, and affordable storage solutions. This overview highlights OE's initiatives to advance technologies from concept to grid validation, diversify beyond lithium-based chemistries to mitigate supply chain risks, and improve bankability.  It discusses emerging use cases—from critical infrastructure resilience to second-order system optimization—alongside enabling tools for valuation, modeling, and decision support. Finally, it recognizes the value of collaboration and expert assistance opportunities for utilities, regulators, industry partners, and other decision-makers to accelerate deployment and ensure affordable access to energy storage solutions.  

Attendees will gain insight into OE's efforts to broaden domestic supply chains, validate next-generation storage systems under real-world conditions, and improve integration of energy storage solutions that strengthen the grid and support national energy objectives. The OE energy storage portfolio, collectively, strives to advance next-generation solutions, strengthen the energy storage ecosystem, and drive system-level innovations to accelerate market readiness and deployment. 

Hosted by Professor Jifeng Liu.

4:00 pm - 5:45 pm The Debut (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Jesse Eisenberg's comedy set in the high-stakes world of community theater finds a shy housewife (Julianne Moore) under the spell of an enigmatic director (Paul Giamatti).

Jesse Eisenberg's sharp, slightly insane take brings us a memorable story of self-actualization through creative destruction. Julianne Moore runs through wild, wonderful extremes as a woman who, having spent her life as a shrinking violet, is determined to make her mark on the world. Paul Giamatti matches her beat for beat as the big-fish-small-pond director who tries to introduce this hapless novice to the liberating potential of the stage—and then both marvels and shudders at what he's created. As the characters change, so too does the world around them, and Eisenberg's deft direction balances both the film's expertly timed comedy and a gorgeous drift into surrealism.

6:00pm In the Evil Day: A Small Town in New Hampshire and the Crime That Stunned the Nation South Danbury Christian Church 1411 Route 4 Danbury NH New Hampshire 03230

On August 19, 1997, in little Colebrook, New Hampshire, a 62-year-old carpenter named Carl Drega, a man with long-simmering property rights grievances, murdered state troopers Scott Phillips and Les Lord at a traffic stop in a supermarket parking lot. Then Drega stole Phillips's cruiser and drove downtown to settle some old scores. By the end of the day three more were dead, Drega among them, and four wounded. Occurring on the eve of America's current plague of gun violence, this tragic event made headlines all over the world and shocked New Hampshire out of a previous innocence. Touching on facets of North Country history, local governance, law enforcement, gun violence, and the human spirit, Richard Adams Carey describes a community that was never a passive victim but rather a brave and resilient survivor. 

Handicap assessable, drinks and food provided

9:00 am Versatile Tote Basket Workshop Chosen Vale Performance Center, Enfield

$70 – $80

Versatile Tote Basket

With Dona Nazarenko

September 19, 2026

9:00 am – 5:00 pm

Meet us in the Chosen Vale Performance Center at the Enfield Shaker Museum to get ready ready for the outdoor “picking” season! This basket is perfect for any of your berry or apple picking needs, or for any hobby, crafting, and gardening needs as well. It is woven with natural and dyed reed, and when not being used it hangs nicely from the attached Shaker tape strap. Class will have reed color choices as well as some Shaker tape color choices available. The final basket will be about 10″ x 5 1/2″ x 7″ high. This is a more advanced style so students should have some basket experience

Who is Doña Nazerenko?

Residing in Tunbridge, Vermont, Doña Nazarenko has been weaving since 1988 and teaching since 1994. While living along the New Jersey coast, Doña developed an interest in woodcrafts and related art forms that developed into her desire to take basket making classes in 1988.

Her exploration of a different art medium has since evolved into a flourishing talent. She now enjoys making traditional baskets using reed with wooden accents to more challenging baskets using birch bark from the area surrounding her current residence in rural Vermont.

The highlight of the early years at her craft was having a one-on-one critique with John McGuire at Peter’s Gallery in 1992. His confidence in her and his discretion continues to help her with her current work. Today she can be seen demonstrating basketry representing Vermont fiber artists at local and out-of-state events. Most days she can be found working in her studio at Country Spirit Baskets

Please bring your own lunch. Water and light refreshments will be provided.

1:30 pm - 3:00 pm Burgundy (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

This documentary explores France's famed wine-growing region through a range of extraordinary characters and a celebration of the pleasure that defines their lives.

In The Truffle Hunters, Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw immersed us in the sensual, slow-paced world of Italian foragers; the macho, high-spirited Gaucho Gaucho provided a wry and personable look at Argentinean cowboys. Now, it's our good fortune to be led by Dweck and Kershaw into another earthy fantasia—the legendary French wine-making region, known as a world capital of pleasure. 

We meet a memorable gallery of Burgundy characters: a landowner obsessed with his family's legacy, an enthusiastic young worker hoping to start his own vineyard, a female apprentice sommelier learning how to talk about wine and a divorced wine critic going on many hapless dates. The breathtaking, formalist compositions offer us a vivid, slightly absurdist celebration of a group of dreamers, who earn both our love and a fair bit of teasing. Underneath the fun, there's social commentary: wherever we go, class and money still hold the upper hand. 

Get more info here.

4 pm - 6 pm Ink (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Danny Boyle directs this adaptation of James Graham's acclaimed play on the rise of media tycoon Rupert Murdoch, starring Guy Pearce, Jack O'Connell and Claire Foy.

In the late 1960s, the millionaire Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) and veteran newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O'Connell) team up to hatch a wild plan: challenge London's leading newspaper with a brash new form of journalism. And they hope to win comeuppance against the snobbish British aristocratic elite. As Lamb reinvents Murdoch's tabloid The Sun, he becomes an attack dog, devolving his newspaper into a sensationalistic, sexually explicit and right-leaning rag—and watches sales skyrocket. 

Academy Award-winning director Danny Boyle (Slumdog Millionaire) works from James Graham's adaptation of his own hit play, taking darkly exuberant comic delight in a wild underdog story with radically destructive results. Claire Foy plays the woman's page editor Jules Davies, and the trio's superb performances, along with Boyle's inventive visual pastiche, make Ink mesmerizing, disturbing entertainment. 

Get more info here.

Join printmaker and multi-media artist Barbara Ackerman in exploring green printmaking techniques using Solarplate, a photo emulsion etching process. 1:30 pm - 3:00 pm Fatherland (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Writer Thomas Mann and his strong-willed daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) embark on a road trip across post-war Germany in Pawel Pawlikowski's meticulous drama.

It's 1949 and the German-born Nobel Prize-winning author Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) is living in the United States, an exile known for his decades of fierce protest against Hitler. After witnessing the brutal descent of his nation into barbarism from afar, he accepts a joint Soviet-US invitation to revisit and give lectures in Germany. Zischler's wondrous performance conveys both Mann's vast humane intellect and his cold, forbidding egotism as he confronts his past and his homeland's sins. Sandra Hüller (Project Hail Mary, Anatomy of a Fall) matches him with her clear-eyed, angrily funny turn as his daughter Erika, who is impatient with the circus that suddenly surrounds her father.

Winning an award for Best Director at Cannes, Paweł Pawlikowski collaborates with screenwriter Hendrik Handloegten (a guest lecturer at Dartmouth this fall!) and cinematographer Łukasz Żal (Hamnet)  to evoke the pain of coming home through the war-ravaged landscapes, which are desolate and yet beautiful: an unforgettable setting for an exquisite film about whether a lost society can heal itself. 

Get more info here.

4 pm - 6 pm Tender Loving Care (Telluride at Dartmouth) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Mike Leigh's expertly crafted portrayal of life in post-Brexit England blends a leveling sense of humor, compassion and finely drawn characters smiling through their struggles.

The indispensable writer-director Mike Leigh, deep into his sixth decade of creating memorable works for theater, television and cinema, has gifted us with an unending stream of compassionate, unflinchingly honest but often funny perspectives of everyday characters in modern England. 

His latest film follows two social workers, Amy (Kate O'Flynn) and Rosie (Alice Bailey Johnson) who face, every day, a harsh reality: most of the people they try to help are too angry and withdrawn to even attempt to heal. Leigh complicates the story of chronically unhappy people with Amy's parents (Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson), whose long happy marriage seems to weather even the insoluble challenges of aging. Though Leigh investigates some bleak corners of British society, he once again works miracles, weaving together his unpredictable combination of pessimism and optimism to bring us, amidst life's sharp corners, profound joy and laughter.

Get more info here.

Abstract: Giant planets are found far more often around metal-rich stars than metal-poor ones, yet most of the Milky Way's stars formed when the typical metallicity was well below solar. Whether those stars could build planets is a question about most of the planets ever formed, and the disks that would answer it are long gone. In this talk, I’ll present how I used thermochemical models to reconstruct what those disks looked like. The chemistry at low metallicity does not simply scale down with the iron content: the balance of oxygen and carbon in the old Galaxy's stars sets how much water ice a disk can make, and the carbon enhancement common among metal-poor stars can leave a disk surprisingly dry, even when it is oxygen-rich relative to iron. I'll then turn to TOI-7019 b, a transiting brown dwarf I discovered orbiting an ancient metal-poor star, and show how these models turn its host's composition into a testable prediction for what JWST should see in its atmosphere. Together, the models and the discovery point to the chemistry of the old Galaxy, and not just its iron content, as what decided where giant planets could form.

Hosted by Professor Elisabeth Newton

5:00 pm - 6:30 pm Freedom & Vigilance: Four Meditations Moore Hall B03

Leela Prasad, St. Purandar Das Distinguished Professor of Religious Studies
Brown University

Tuesday, September 22, 2026
5:00 PM
Location: Moore B03 (tentative)
Free and open to all

Reception to follow

Lecture title: Freedom & Vigilance: Four Meditations

Abstract: In a deepening climate of erosion and erasure, we must keep asking what each of us can do to resist inhumanity, fear, and disenchantment, and to keep searching for more livable futures. This talk offers four meditations—on the forest, the sanctuary, the carceral web, and the heart—to discern a practice of vigilance more sovereign and sustaining than the brute vigilantism of the state and other oppressive structures. What does it mean to be alert to threat, but also to be vigilant for justice; vigilant for the smallest acts of dignity; vigilant for freedom in the ordinary and the everyday? What forms of agency does an ethics of vigilance reveal? What hope does it trace, what freedom does it offer, and what does it demand of us?

The James and David Orr Memorial Lectures on Culture and Religion bring to Dartmouth each year scholars and writers whose achievements are at the highest level, but whose main fields of interest are not necessarily religion. Past Orr Lecturers include historians, anthropologists, novelists, biologists, and philosophers.

6:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution Fuller Public Library 29 School Street Hillsboro New Hampshire 03244

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

"Mary was well prepared and is a wonderful educator and speaker. She knows her subject well and her enthusiasm was evident. The slides and stories she chose were perfect for the subject and we could tell she knows a lot more than she could cram into the presentation. Mary is a valuable resource for learning NH history."

- Previous HTG host

Parking is across the street from the library and handicap parking is available in the front of the building as well as the back. A handicap lift inside accesses all levels of the library.

7:00pm African American Soldiers and Sailors of New Hampshire During the American Revolution Gordon-Nash Library 69 Main St New Hampton NH 03256

One of the most interesting aspects of the American Revolution is the role played by African Americans in the fight for independence. Both free African Americans and those that were enslaved were key in manning state militias and Continental Army units, as well as serving on the high seas in the Navy and on privately armed ships. Indeed, their service to the colonies was crucial in a conflict that lasted nearly seven years. Prohibited from serving in military units and largely considered "undesirable elements," how is it that these African-American soldiers came to fight for the cause of liberty, even when their own personal liberty was not guaranteed?

Glenn Knoblock examines the history of African-American soldiers' service during the war, including how and why they enlisted, their interaction with white soldiers, service on the battlefields, how they were perceived by the enemy and the officers under whom they served, and their treatment after the war. 

Street parking; limited parking at the side entrance. Accessible from the side entrance without stairs. A sidewalk leads from the street to the side entrance. Light refreshments will be served at the program.

The SWC is excited to bring you a mid-week restorative practice* with to-go healthy snacks and journals!

This experiential learning opportunity will take place every Wednesday from 3:30 to 4:15pm. Each session will look something like this: 
- Setup mats and settle into our spaces (5- minutes)

- Prompted free-write in provided journals (6 minutes)
- Debrief and optional sharing time (6 min) 
- Ending session and putting away mats, journals (3 minutes) 

*mats will be provided

What is Yoga Nidra?

Yoga nidra is a type of meditation practice originating from ancient India, commonly known as "yogic sleep" or "dynamic sleep." It is a contemplative practice that involves following guided prompts while lying in a comfortable position through various stages of relaxation, breathing exercises, and visualization.

This practice aims to induce a state of deep relaxation and meditation, similar to the liminal state between waking and sleeping. This state can provide numerous physical, emotional, and mental benefits, such as reducing stress and anxiety, improving sleep, enhancing creativity, and promoting overall well-being. In this state, you may experience a sense of timelessness, expansiveness, and interconnectedness.

4:00 pm - 5:30 pm Monstrous Conceptions: A History of Race, Disability, and Reproductive Medicine Carson Hall L01

Join the Department of History in welcoming historian Miriam Rich to discuss her work Monstrous Conceptions: A History of Race, Disability, and Reproductive Medicine in the United States. (New York: Columbia University Press, 2026).

This talk explores the history of “monstrous birth” in modern U.S. medical science, tracing the practices and ideas that transformed newborn bodies into scientific specimens of monstrosity. Recast as a biological phenomenon, the monster gained new social and cultural salience across the nineteenth- and early twentieth-century United States. Monstrosity gave form to pervasive anxieties about the meaning of racial difference, the fragility of racial descent, and the volatility of women’s reproduction—and contributed to ideas about deviant and defective bodies that still haunt us today.

Professor Miriam Rich is a historian of U.S. medicine, science, and health, currently assistant professor at University of Texas Medical Branch, (Department of Bioethics and Health Humanities), where she holds the James Wade Rockwell Professorship in Philosophy of Medicine. Her research explores the troubled history of “monstrous birth” as a category in modern medical science, revealing how historical practices produced enduring ideas about human difference. Her writing appears in journals such as Bulletin of the History of Medicine, The Lancet, Isis, Gender & History, New Genetics and Society, and Revista Ciência & Saúde Coletiva.

Find out more about Monstrous Conceptions: https://cup.columbia.edu/book/monstrous-conceptions/9780231200325/.

All are welcome.

5 pm - 6 pm On Burke's Conservatism with Greg Collins, Yale Univeristy Room 003, Rockefeller Center

Edmund Burke is often seen as the founding father of modern conservatism. How is his “conservatism” similar to or different from what we call conservatism in our own time? Prof. Gregory M. Collins—Lecturer and Director of Undergraduate Studies in the Program on Ethics, Politics, and Economics at Yale—is well placed to address this question. An award-winning teacher and scholar, his research ranges widely over the origins of liberalism and conservatism. His book Commerce and Manners in Edmund Burke’s Political Economy appeared with Cambridge in 2020, and his book on the idea of civil society in early African-American political thought will appear in February, 2027.

6 pm - 7 pm Comparing AIs and the Human Brain: the Challenge of Agency Kemeny Hall 008

https://math.dartmouth.edu/photos/rotate/prosser-poster-mumford-sep-2026.pdf

Abstract: AIs started with "neural nets" in the 1940's, inspired by neurons, and the brain continues to have many parallels to AI with the introduction of transformers and scalability. I believe that future AIs will benefit by borrowing more ideas from the brain and from human life. Looking at human development, it is not until age 18 (or 21) that people are considered adults, hence given rights to act as they wish. They are then given AGENCY, to plan and take actions in the world freely. Silicon Valley today assumes that limited agency can be grafted on large language models easily. But is that true? The purpose of this talk is to analyze what seems to be missing.

7:00pm Live Free or Die: The Contested History of the Words on Your License Plate Bristol Historic Town Hall Summer Street Bristol NH 03222

In 1969, when New Hampshire officials decided to put the state’s motto – “live free or die” – on its license plates, many citizens viewed the act as an endorsement of the deeply unpopular war being waged in Vietnam and protested by covering up or altering the motto. In response, authorities cracked down hard: arresting, fining, and sometimes even incarcerating those who engaged in duct-tape dissent. People appealed their convictions, sparking a legal contest over the First Amendment that went all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court. In this multimedia presentation, historian and former newspaper reporter Dan Billin tells a uniquely New Hampshire tale illustrating the genius – and the fragility – of the First Amendment.

12:15 pm - 1:00 pm Research Talk – Chris Sollars: The Neighbors 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center

All dates: Sep 24, Oct 15

This Research Talk will feature Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies Lydia Jennings, Associate Professor of Environmental Studies Theresa Ong, and Research Associate of Environmental Studies Martha Torstenson, and the talk will take place in the 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center. This programming coincides with a faculty exhibition by Associate Professor of Studio Art Chris Sollars, The Neighbors, a new body of work inspired by coexistence and inquiry.

Set in rural Vermont, The Neighbors is a multimedia video installation about the non-human inhabitants of the lands around the artist’s home. After over two decades living in San Francisco, California, Sollars moved to Vermont in the fall of 2024. To get to know his new home and neighbors, he has spent the past two years interacting with his surroundings through slow listening and observation, learning them spatially and temporally.  This intentional gathering of information has taken the form of diaristic snapshots taken throughout the seasons, field recordings, the collection of discarded nests and materials, and the placement of wildlife cameras in the open woodland edges of his home, which neighbors a land trust, a national forest, and the Appalachian Trail.

The Neighbors is on view from Sept. 15 – Nov. 8, 2026.
