Sep 24 Oct 15
2 pm - 3 pm PhD Thesis Defense: Shu Huang academic Rm 232, Cummings Hall (Jackson Conf Rm)/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Clostridium thermocellum is a promising organism for consolidated bioprocessing of lignocellulosic biomass because it can both solubilize cellulose and ferment the released sugars. However, achieving high ethanol titers remains challenging. One potential limitation is the native NADH-linked alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) reaction, which becomes increasingly thermodynamically unfavorable as ethanol accumulates. This thesis investigated an alternative ethanol production strategy in which reduced ferredoxin is used to generate NADPH through a ferredoxin:NADP+ oxidoreductase (Fnor), and ethanol formation is driven by an NADPH-linked ADH reaction.

To establish this pathway, candidate Fnor enzymes were first screened for cofactor specificity, catalytic activity, thermostability, and expression in C. thermocellum. Selected Fnor enzymes were then tested in engineered C. thermocellum strains for their effects on ethanol production. The complete NADPH-linked pathway was subsequently reconstructed in vitro using purified enzymes to determine whether pyruvate could be converted to ethanol through the proposed reaction sequence and whether the pathway remained functional at high ethanol concentrations. Finally, the pathway was incorporated into an engineered C. thermocellum background designed to reduce competing electron-sink reactions. Carbon monoxide (CO) adaptation was used to inhibit hydrogenase activity, increase the availability of reduced ferredoxin for FNOR reaction, and improve strain growth under CO.

Multiple thermostable, NADPH-specific Fnor enzymes were identified and successfully expressed in C. thermocellum, and several increased ethanol production relative to an empty-vector control. The reconstructed enzyme pathway converted pyruvate to ethanol with 100% conversion in vitro and remained active in the presence of up to 1 M ethanol. In vivo, CO-adapted strain expression the Fnor enzyme Hth_1218 and AdhEAP125 showed substantially increased ethanol production, with titers increasing from approximately 60 mM to approximately 200 mM from 50 g/L cellobiose.

Together, these results demonstrate that a NADPH-linked ethanol production pathway can function both in vitro and in C. thermocellum. This work establishes an alternative pathway for ethanol production in C. thermocellum and provides a foundation for further engineering toward higher ethanol titers

Thesis Committee: Daniel G. Olson (chair), Lee R. Lynd, Margaret E. Ackerman, Carolyn E. Lubner (National Laboratory of the Rockies)

Investors, developers, and scholars debate whether capital flowing into fusion, geothermal, and other frontier energy tech signals real breakthroughs or another bubble—and what past cycles reveal about who wins and loses in the energy transition.

Panel 2 | Beyond the Bottleneck: Financing the Grid America Needs Now

6:00pm A Walk Back in Time: The Secrets of Cellar Holes Woodstock Town Office Building 165 Lost River Road N. Woodstock New Hampshire 03262

Northern New England is full of reminders of past lives: stone walls, old foundations, a century-old lilac struggling to survive as the forest reclaims a once-sunny dooryard. What forces shaped settlement, and later abandonment, of these places? Adair Mulligan explores the rich story to be discovered in what remains behind. See how one town has set out to create an inventory of its cellar holes, piecing together the clues in the landscape. Such a project can help landowners know what to do if they have archaeological sites on their land and help stimulate interest in a town's future through its past.

6:30pm Covered Bridges of New Hampshire - Past and Present Daland Memorial Library 8 Lilac Lane Mont Vernon NH 03057

New Hampshire was once home to over 300 covered bridges. Today, there are over sixty authentic covered bridges in New Hampshire, forty-six of which are over a century old. These bridges exist solely because of the efforts of a small but powerful community that both recognized their significance and honored their tradition. Join author and photographer Kim Varney Chandler as she shares an overview of covered bridges in the Granite State, along with interesting facts she uncovered while researching her 2022 book, Covered Bridges of New Hampshire. Learn more about both existing and lost covered bridges in your area.

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm Development of mRNAs for cellular localization of therapeutics to treat diseases Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 937 4316 0035
Passcode: 411385

Genetic medicines have the potential to treat various diseases, but require development of controlled delivery vehicles to transfect specific cell types in specific organs to achieve therapeutic effects. Moreover, certain ailments including inflammatory diseases and cancer would benefit from control over intracellular and extracellular localization of therapeutic proteins.

In this presentation, I will discuss the development of selective organ targeting (SORT) lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) that enable high levels of genome editing in the liver, lungs, spleen, tumors, or bone marrow. I will also discuss signal peptide engineered nucleic acid design (SEND) mRNAs that encode for etanercept/TNF-α inhibitor antibodies and demonstrate therapeutic efficacy in a psoriasis model by reducing hyperkeratosis and inflammation. The modular nature of SEND enables intracellular and extracellular localization control of various functional proteins for diverse therapeutic applications. Cumulatively, these findings introduce strategies to control how delivery nanoparticles navigate to where they need to go, control how delivery nanoparticles release nucleic acids inside of cells, and control how translated proteins navigate to where they need to go for ultimate therapeutic benefit.

Sep 25 – Nov 14, 2026 Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee | Jason Pappas Main Gallery- AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Opening Reception Friday, September 25, 5-7 PM through November 14, 2026 | Linda Bryan; Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan; Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee; Jason Pappas (Linda Bryan; Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan on separate event page)

We are pleased to present four distinct but interconnected exhibitions that explore how we understand the past, navigate uncertainty, and carry traces of history into the present. Through photography, painting, drawing, assemblage, and sculpture, the artists consider memory, place, family, perception, and the enduring relationship between people and the materials and environments they inhabit.

E. N. Wennberg Gallery: Mapping Uncertainty features Andrea Kantrowitz and Jeesoo Lee, whose practices meet in their exploration of perception, transformation, displacement, and change. Kantrowitz’s expansive sumi ink landscapes, informed by the Hudson Valley and Chinese literati painting, evoke environments that are simultaneously familiar and elusive. Lee’s delicate assemblages of translucent paper and thread occupy a more intimate scale, reflecting experiences of hesitation, displacement, belonging, and connection. Although their approaches differ, both artists embrace uncertainty not as an obstacle to overcome, but as a productive condition in which new possibilities can emerge. Their shared artistic history, dating back to a 2009 exhibition, gives the current presentation an added sense of continuity and renewed dialogue.

Rebecca Lawrence Gallery Entry: Jason Pappas’s Relics from the Human Age turns to the physical landscape as a record of human history and intention. Working with trees that fell on his Vermont property, Pappas discovered not only a source of material but traces of the people who had shaped the land before him. The property’s gardens, plantings, workshop, and remnants of earlier woodworking reveal layers of labor, foresight, and care extending across generations. By transforming salvaged wood into new works, Pappas carries these histories forward without attempting to recreate them exactly. The resulting objects function simultaneously as sculpture, artifact, and continuation—reminders that actions taken by one generation can shape lives far into the future.

Taken together, these four exhibitions offer a meditation on what remains: the photograph that outlives the memory, the painting that transforms recollection, the landscape that shifts beneath our feet, and the material traces left behind by those who came before us. Each exhibition approaches the past differently, yet all four ask us to consider how histories are preserved, altered, inherited, and reimagined. Across these varied practices, the artists suggest that looking backward is not simply an act of remembrance, can be a way of understanding where we are now and imagining what we might carry forward.

Sep 25 – Nov 14, 2026 Linda Bryan | Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan Main Gallery- AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

Sessions start 10:00 am · Free

Opening Reception Friday, September 25, 5-7 PM through November 14, 2026 | Linda Bryan; Jim Jordan & Rachel Jordan; Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee; Jason Pappas (Andrea Kantrowitz & Jeesoo Lee; Jason Pappas on separate event page)

We are pleased to present four distinct but interconnected exhibitions that explore how we understand the past, navigate uncertainty, and carry traces of history into the present. Through photography, painting, drawing, assemblage, and sculpture, the artists consider memory, place, family, perception, and the enduring relationship between people and the materials and environments they inhabit.

Elizabeth Rowland Mayor Gallery: In Falling Leaves, Linda Bryan examines the fragile relationship between memory and evidence. Drawing from family photographs, documents, objects, and ephemera, Bryan considers how the stories we inherit—and the stories we tell ourselves—can shift over time. A childhood photograph, a handwritten note, and other fragments of family history become points of departure for questioning what is remembered, what is forgotten, and what remains when direct access to the past begins to disappear. The resulting works form an intimate and incomplete family archive, suggesting that personal history is not fixed, but continually reconstructed from the fragments that survive.

Clifford B. West Gallery: Past Forward brings together the work of Jim Jordan and Rachel Jordan in a dialogue between memory, observation, history, and abstraction. Jim Jordan draws on recollections of childhood and adolescence in the 1940s and 1950s, transforming those memories through the visual language of Modernism. Rachel Jordan approaches the still life through a contemporary lens, engaging with a rich history of artistic traditions while exploring the relationships among objects, space, form, and perception. Together, their paintings demonstrate how the past can be revisited and transformed rather than simply remembered, allowing personal experience, art history, and abstraction to generate new ways of seeing the present.

Taken together, these four exhibitions offer a meditation on what remains: the photograph that outlives the memory, the painting that transforms recollection, the landscape that shifts beneath our feet, and the material traces left behind by those who came before us. Each exhibition approaches the past differently, yet all four ask us to consider how histories are preserved, altered, inherited, and reimagined. Across these varied practices, the artists suggest that looking backward is not simply an act of remembrance, can be a way of understanding where we are now and imagining what we might carry forward.

1:00pm Sustainability: An American Literary History Remick Country Doctor Museum and Farm 58 Cleveland Hill Rd Tamworth NH 03886

What is sustainability? And how has American literature shaped our understanding of this concept, in ways both surprising and disturbing? This interactive program begins with a discussion of current ideas about sustainability. Then, we will go back in time to examine Thomas Jefferson's vision of American agricultural abundance, which he contrasted with an overpopulated and under-resourced Europe. Throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries, writers such as Walt Whitman and Charlotte Perkins Gilman drew on Jefferson's agrarian vision to respond to sustainability crises of their time. But in so doing, they depicted selective breeding and racial "improvement" as the solution to population crises and the path to agricultural plenty. We will explore this particularly eugenic conception of sustainability and discuss what new or different versions of sustainability might prove more useful in our current moment.

Humanities to GoAbby GoodeRemick Country Doctor Museum and FarmJames Cruickshank, jcruickshank@remickmuseum.org

1:00 pm Lia Rothstein Workshop: Biomaterial and Sculpture Installation AVA Gallery and Art Center, Lebanon

All dates: Sep 26, Oct 3, Oct 17

$25

Hands-on Community Biomaterial Workshop and Sculpture Installation with Lia Rothstein | North Studio

Dates: Saturday Sept 26, 1-3 PM

Saturday Oct 3, 1-3 PM

Saturday Oct 17, 1-3 PM

Must be 12 years old or older to participate

Teens under 16 should be accompanied by an adult

Exhibitions Program Workshop: Suggested donation: $25 pp

Workshop overview: This workshop emphasizes community engagement, collective creativity, and ecological responsibility, while encouraging participants to consider how art can strengthen connections between people, place, and the environment. Explore the creative possibilities of sustainable art through the design and creation of an ephemeral art installation made from innovative, natural, and biodegradable biomaterials. In this hands-on workshop, participants will investigate how organic materials can be transformed into temporary artworks that celebrate the beauty of impermanence while fostering environmental awareness.

Working collaboratively as a group, under the guidance of instructor Lia Rothstein, participants will learn about a sustainable material made from re-purposed crustacean shells and develop a site-responsive installation that will evolve and naturally decompose over time outside in AVA’s sculpture garden. Together we will create translucent biodegradable sculptural pieces and then hang them where we can observe how our pieces change over time while interacting with elements of rain, sun, wind, and temperature. Ultimately, if Nature cooperates, our installation will biodegrade while nourishing the trees and plants underneath it along the way!

Session One – Learn how to use a sustainable and biodegradable biomaterial, made from crab shells (!), to create some pieces that will be used for sculptures, color the material using a plant-based and non-toxic colorant (2 hours)

Session Two – Using our (now) dried biomaterial pieces, decorate and fabricate small sculptures. (2 hours) These will be hung in AVA’s Sculpture Garden in our final session.

Session Three – Work collaboratively to create a sculptural installation with our prepared biomaterial elements in the Sculpture Garden. (2 hours)

Participants should bring: apron to cover clothes, nitrile gloves that fit their hands, notebook/pen or pencil.

Lia Rothstein has BA and MFA degrees from Boston University. She has been a professional photographer and artist for over 40 years and has taught photography and mixed media classes throughout New England and internationally. Lia was awarded artist residencies at the Vermont Studio Center, the Baer Art Center in Hofsos, Iceland, and the Brattleboro Vermont Museum and Art Center. She has exhibited her photographic and mixed media work in galleries and museums across the US and her work is in numerous collections, including the Polaroid International Exhibition Photography Collection, and the collections of John Hancock and the Radisson Group. Rothstein’s encaustic and cold wax paintings are featured in the book, “Cold Wax Medium: Techniques, Concepts and Conversations” by Rebecca Crowell and Jerry McLaughlin and other publications. Lia is a member of New England Wax, a regional juried organization, the national and regional branches of the Surface Design Association, and the International Sculpture Center.

2:00pm From Mickey to Magoo: The Golden Age of American Animation The Flying Monkey Theater, owned by Pemi Valley Habitat for Humanity 39 Main St Plymouth NH 03264

From the 1920s to the 1960s, adult American theatergoers could anticipate a cartoon before each feature film. From Mickey Mouse to Donald Duck, Popeye, Betty Boop, Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tom and Jerry, Mighty Mouse, Casper the Friendly Ghost, and Mr. Magoo, the beloved cartoon "stars" were every bit as memorable as the Hollywood actors who shared the marquee. Many of these cartoons were redistributed as Saturday morning shows for kids of the next generation.

Margo Burns offers an introduction to the people and studios that made these films and the changing technology, aesthetics, music, politics, and economics behind them, showing stills, characters, and clips from many of these beautifully hand-drawn films. At the end of her program, participants are treated to one of the classics in its entirety. 

The venue is fully accessible. There is parking available and on Sundays it is free. There will be pre-registration.

4 pm - 7 pm The Odyssey (DFS: Myths Revisited) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Stellar performances by Matt Damon and an A-list ensemble make Christopher Nolan's blockbuster adaptation of Homer's epic an unmissable cinematic event.

Matt Damon gives the performance of his career as Odysseus, the trickster whose equine gift won the Trojan war for the Greeks after ten years of battle and siege. Homer's epic poem follows our hero's ten-year journey home, as the gods, angered by his duplicity and ingratitude, send storms and monsters his way. Only Athena (Zendaya) seems to offer guidance rather than grievances.

Meanwhile, back home his wife (Anne Hathaway), son (Tom Holland) and loyal servant (John Leguizamo) must negotiate with dozens of unwelcome suitors, led by the scheming Antinous (Robert Pattinson). Lupita N'yongo, Elliot Page, Benny Safdie, Jon Bernthal, Charlize Theron and Samantha Morton round out the A-list cast of Trojan war characters who haunt Odysseus and enchantresses who stand between him and home.

Rather than view Odysseus's hubris as boastful and ungrateful, Nolan positions the Greek warrior's fatal flaw as his failure to surrender to forces beyond his control and tendency to shoulder too much responsibility. The result is a realist yet majestic interpretation of the classic myth, which swells with primal human feeling, thrilling action, meticulous scoring and dazzling visuals. The Odyssey lives up to the "epic" moniker in what may be the cinema event of the decade.

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited"

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm Who Makes Peace Now? Diplomacy, Conflict, and the Changing International World Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

In 2025, the world documented the highest number of conflicts since World War II, an uptick in both interstate wars and intra-state conflicts over the last decade. What is driving the increase in organized violence and are we seeing a commensurate rise in conflict prevention and management efforts by the United States and the international community? 

The Dickey Center welcomes leading experts in international conflict management and peacebuilding to address these questions.

Former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Anne Witkowsky has spent more than 30 years working on conflict issues, from security in Europe to counter-terrorism to strengthening stability in fragile states. She has held senior roles at the National Security Council, Department of Defense, the State Department, and think tanks. She is a senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, DC. 

Professor Elizabeth McClintock '86, Ph.D., has worked on peacebuilding efforts worldwide and advised policymakers at the World Bank, United Nations and multiple governments, as well as the community members most impacted by war and its resolution. She is the Executive Director at the Bridgeway Group, teaches at Harvard Law School and at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. She is in residence at Dartmouth as the Magro Family Distinguished Fellow in International Affairs at the Dickey Center.

This panel will explore the current trends, address the thorny questions facing those trying to prevent international conflicts, and the factors that contribute to successful efforts for peace. Ms. Witkowsky and Prof. McClintock will bring different perspectives to the conversation, helping to elucidate the challenges at the national level, as well as those facing peacebuilding efforts from the ground up.

The conversation will be moderated by Dickey Center Director Victoria K. Holt.

5:30pm Last of the Granite State Rattlesnakes Abbott Library 11 Soonipi Circle Sunapee NH 03782

Rattlesnakes were so common in colonial-era New Hampshire that dozens of places were named for them, ranging from the Massachusetts border to the White Mountains. They were so abundant some settlers could pay their property taxes with the bounties offered for killing them. Today, however, Crotalus horridus, the timber rattlesnake, is the state’s rarest native animal—only a handful are known to survive. State law protects them now, but that may not be enough to save them. Wildlife biologists have predicted this tiny remnant will die out without extraordinary intervention.

How did this feared and fascinating animal come to the very brink of extirpation in our state? This illustrated presentation maps how we got here through the social, political, and natural history of New Hampshire’s rattlesnakes. Historian and former newspaper reporter Dan Billin presents vivid, little-known stories and images from our centuries-long war on our rattlesnakes. Topics include who’s been bitten; the medicinal use of rattlesnake oil by the Shakers and others; the exploits of the “Rattlesnake King of New Hampshire”; the twentieth-century rattlesnake panic in the legislature; and the mysterious recent appearance of rattlesnakes with Pennsylvania genes. This program reviews what is and isn’t being done today to conserve our rattlesnakes, and the many obstacles to their survival.

Humanities to GoDan BillinAbbott LibraryAbbott Library, info@abbottlibrary.org

10:00am Uprooted: Heartache and Hope in New Hampshire Calumet Lutheran Ministries 1090 Ossipee Lake Road Freedom NH 03836

Uprooted is a 30-minute documentary based on interviews collected during New Hampshire Humanities' Fences & Neighbors initiative on immigration. It tells the story of five refugees who escaped from war-torn countries to resettle in New Hampshire. The film explores what it means to be a refugee and how it feels to make a new life in a strange place, often without English language skills, family, a job, or community contacts. The film leaves us pondering questions of belonging and citizenship. What does it mean to be an American? Once a refugee, are you destined always to be a refugee? What are our responsibilities toward one another? A New Hampshire Humanities presenter introduces the film and leads a post-film discussion.

 

Program (part of the Fruits & Roots Retreat) will be held in the new Oasis Building behind the Conference Center. Parking in the Conference Cetner lot or at the Oasis. Handicap accessible. No registration required. All are welcome.

5:30 pm - 6:30 pm Geoeconomics Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

The world economy is undergoing the largest change since the end of the Cold War. Professor Maggiori's lecture will explain how governments apply geoeconomic pressure using their economies' trade and financial relationships. He will discuss chokepoints in global finance and supply chains, how governments use tariffs, sanctions, and export controls to apply pressure, and the implications for building a prosperous economic order.

The event is free and open to the public, but registration is required. It will also be recorded and liverstreamed. 

Matteo Maggiori is the Moghadam Family Professor of Finance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business. His research focuses on international economics and finance.  He is a co-founder and director of the GCAP Lab. His research topics have included the analysis of exchange rates under imperfect capital markets, geoeconomics, the international monetary system, reserve currencies, tax havens, very long-run discount rates and climate change, and expectations and portfolio investment. His research combines theory and data with the aim of improving international economic policy. He is a faculty research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, where he organizes the NBER International Economics and Geopolitics (IEG) meeting, and a research affiliate at the Center for Economic Policy Research. He received his PhD from the University of California at Berkeley. Among a number of honors, he is the recipient of the Fischer Black Prize awarded to an outstanding financial economist under the age of 40, the Carnegie and Guggenheim fellowships, and the Bernacer Prize for outstanding contributions in macroeconomics and finance by a European economist under age 40.

Sponsored by the International Security and Economics Pilot, the Davidson Institute for Global Security at the Dickey Center for International Understanding, The Michael G. Fisch 1983 Academic Cluster on Globalization, and The Center for Business, Government & Society at the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth.

This program explores some of the most urgent moral challenges that Artificial Intelligence presents to society today. Topics include automation and job displacement, deepfakes and misinformation, the role of AI in education, implicit bias, autonomous systems (such as self-driving cars and drones), and the ethical implications of a potential technological singularity. After a brief introduction to applied ethics and the technology behind generative AI, we will examine each issue in turn, highlighting the core moral questions they raise and their significance for shaping sound policies and regulations. The session will conclude with an open discussion, giving attendees a chance to share perspectives and ask questions. Participants will come away with a clearer understanding of the ethical landscape of AI and the tools to think critically about its future impact.

¿Ser o no ser? What does it truly mean "to be" in a world that looks the other way?

Playful, powerful and joyful—a radical reimagining of Shakespeare's Hamlet, featuring eight actors with Down syndrome. Versions of the original text intermingle with personal anecdotes from the cast in a provocative dialogue that brings us face to face with the themes of empathy, exclusion and the irrepressible human spirit. The high-energy performance upends the Shakespearean focus on the individual—here, the melancholic Prince—and instead centers community.

Hailed across its runs at Lincoln Center, Theatre for a New Audience and the Edinburgh International Festival, the pioneering work from Peruvian theater company Teatro La Plaza now lands at the Hop, pulsing with life and classic lessons we desperately need to relearn today.

4:00 pm - 4:45 pm A SPACE FOR DIALOGUE GALLERY TALK Hood Museum of Art

Class, Community, and Commute: Representations of Private and Public Travel in the Late 19th and 20th Centuries

The museum's Mellon Special Project Intern Javier Baluyut ’26 will discuss his student-curated exhibition that explores depictions of travel in the late 19th and 20th centuries through the lens of American culture and class. Travel is a ubiquitous human experience, with the modern age broadening available transportation to a range inconceivable less than a century ago. American travel culture has likewise evolved to serve the needs of its modern population, supporting a vast nest of public roads and highways at odds with a sparse passenger railway and underdeveloped public transportation networks.

5 pm - 6 pm Cuba and the United States:What Lies Ahead? Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

Since taking office in 2025, the Trump administration has portrayed Cuba as a national security threat to the United States, pledging to “use every tool at our disposal” to counteract the government there, including regime change.  While the U.S. and Cuba have been at odds for decades, this approach includes an increase in political and economic pressures, including limitations on oil and increased sanctions. 
 
Former U.S. Ambassadors Jeffrey DeLaurentis and Peter DeShazo ’69 will discuss the recent evolution of the U.S./Cuba relationship, the variables in play in that dynamic, increased U.S. sanctions and other forms of pressure, the effects of those measures and possible future outcomes.

Moderated by Desirée J. Garcia, Chair, Department of Latin American, Latino, & Caribbean Studies.

6:00pm Rethinking the U.S. National Parks Kimball Library 5 Academy Avenue Atkinson NH 03811

In the famous words of Wallace Stegner, “national parks are the best idea we ever had. Absolutely American, absolutely democratic, they reflect us at our best rather than our worst." But are National Parks truly “democratic”? Who has access to National Parks and what kinds of fantasies do they serve? This interactive program explores the history of U.S. National Parks—as myths, symbols of democratic ideals, and colonial spaces—alongside today’s common National Park activities. Why are visitation rates on the rise? What are we seeking at the National Parks? What do our National Park consumption habits tell us about ourselves? We will look at the rising phenomenon of “selfie deaths,” as well as the broader role of social media in National Park consumption. National Parks may represent freedom for some, but no matter how carefully tended and regulated, they also form part of a planet in crisis. How does climate change fundamentally threaten National Parks, challenging their status as highly valued, protectable spaces? How might we revise the preservation tradition that gave birth to the National Parks to include our own neighborhoods and communities? We will consider these questions in the national context, but also in light of our own state—home to the White Mountain National Forest, which attracts so many eager visitors every year.

The event has plenty of parking and the building is accessible. Please register so we can plan accordingly.

Oct 2 – Oct 4, 2026 Writer’s Retreat Weekend Enfield Shaker Museum

$230 – $700

Writer’s Retreat Weekend

October 2-4, 2026

Set against the quiet beauty and rich history of the Enfield Shaker Museum, this intimate Writer’s Retreat Weekend, October 2–4, offers a rare opportunity to learn, write, and connect. Designed for writers of all levels. This immersive experience brings together three accomplished, published authors—Janis Robinson Daly, James Nehring, and Gail Ward Olmsted—for a weekend of creativity, exploration, and professional insight.

Participants will enjoy a thoughtfully curated schedule of workshops, discussions, and shared experiences:

Friday, October 2
The weekend begins with check-in at 12:00 PM, followed by a 3:30–5:00 pm Meet & Greet and Writers Workshop led by Janis Robinson Daly. This engaging session will include prompts and writing exercises designed to inspire creativity and encourage writers. Each writer will explore styles beyond their usual genres.
Dinner will be served at 6:00 pm. Followed by at 7:00 PM by An Evening of Readings and Book Sale and Signing at the Chosen Vale Performance Center. This event is open to the public.

Saturday, October 3
You will start your day with an Adventure Walk from 7:30–8:30 am led by James Nehring. He will be  offering a reflective experience.  This will be centered on finding inspiration in the world around us. Breakfast follows from 9:00–9:45 am.
From 10:00 am–12:00 pm, Nehring will lead a memoir writing workshop. This will  focusing on research techniques and balancing fact with narrative. Lunch will be served from 12:30–1:00 pm.
In the afternoon, from 1:30–3:30 pm, Gail Ward Olmsted will host a marketing and branding workshop. Guiding writers through the essentials of building an author platform and connecting with readers.
From 4:00–5:30 PM, Janis Robinson Daly returns with a second writing workshop filled with prompts and creative exploration. Dinner is at 6:00 pm, followed by Participant Readings at 7:00 pm—an encouraging space to share work and celebrate creativity.

Sunday, October 4
The final day begins with breakfast from 7:30–8:00 am. From 8:30–10:00 am, Janis Robinson Daly will lead a Publishing Workshop. She will be offering insight into the many paths to publication and practical steps for moving forward. The weekend concludes with a Wrap-up Session at 10:30 am.

 For those seeking a fully immersive experience, overnight accommodations are available in the historic Great Stone Dwelling. All meals will be provided. Evening gatherings and shared meals create a warm, welcoming atmosphere that fosters creativity and community.

Whether you join for the full weekend or workshops and meals, this limited-capacity retreat offers inspiration and professional guidance. This weekend will give you the chance to deepen your writing practice in a truly unique setting

About the Authors

Janis Robinson Daly

Splitting her time between Cape Cod, NH, NJ, and snowbird destinations, a tablet becomes Janis Robinson Daly’s library and desk, packed for reading and writing, wherever she might land. Inspired by the discovery that an ancestor founded the Woman’s Medical College of PA, Daly’s first two novels, The Unlocked Path and The Path Beneath Her Feet, celebrates pioneering women doctors in the first half of the 20th century. Her third book, Under Two Flags, is a retelling of a memoir of a young Boston woman who travels to Berlin in 1916 to study opera. Daly’s grandfather, Eliot H. Robinson, Sr. ghost-wrote the original memoir in 1918.

Daly graduated with a B.A. in Psychology from Wheaton College, at the time, a women’s college. At Wheaton, she developed a heightened awareness of female-centric issues. She went on to a career in consumer marketing and sales before turning a love of history into a second chapter. Her annual literary citizenship program, #31titleswomeninhistory, has gained recognition as an innovative way to celebrate Women’s History Month in March. Website: www.janisrdaly.com

James Nehring

James Nehring loves a good adventure, and he doesn’t let his fear of heights, risk, and speed get in the way.

Author of eight books, he’s appeared on National Public Radio and CNN. His essays have appeared in the Boston Globe, Washington Post and Chicago Tribune. Recipient of a Fulbright award and a career in education, he most recently served as a professor at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. He lives in central Massachusetts with his wife, Laurie, and two cats standing in for three kids who’ve flown the coop. When he’s not teaching, writing, or volunteering around town, you can find him outdoors on his bike or trekking through the woods just a few steps from his kitchen door. Website: www.jamesnehring.com Substack: “The Daily Adventure” jamesnehring.substack.com

Gail Ward Olmsted

Gail Ward Olmsted was a marketing executive and a college professor before she began writing fiction on a full-time basis. A trip to Sedona, AZ inspired her first novel, Jeep Tour. Three more novels followed, including Landscape of a Marriage, a biographical fiction featuring landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted, a distant cousin of her husband’s, and his wife Mary. Her latest books are a trio of legal dramas featuring a former district attorney trying to salvage her once promising career: Miranda Writes, Miranda Nights and Miranda Fights.

Olmsted enjoys writing about quirky, wonderful women in search of a second chance at a happy ever after. When not writing, she loves being on the water, especially in a kayak. She is well known for her blonde brownies and coffee is her love language. Website: gailwardolmsted.com

A special 4-week lecture series!

Join David Bisno for a spirited discussion of the complicated relationships between Iranians, Americans, and the English. What was the path by which American hubris, ineptitude, delusions, and catastrophic miscalculations led to the present situation? What part did oil, Communists, Israelis, shahs, and an Islamic God play in the story? We will unveil not a single error but a pattern of English greed and American inattentiveness, bureaucratic in-fighting, and a string of strategic blunders allowing unnecessary crises to become a historic rupture with worldwide repercussions. 

David Bisno, a retired ophthalmologist with degrees from Harvard, Dartmouth, and the Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis), has, for the past 33 years, developed and presented courses on a myriad of subjects for ILEAD/Osher and for other institutes for lifelong learning across this country and overseas. He is known for clear, fair, nuanced presentations of provocative, complicated topics, engaging his students with energy and enthusiasm. He looks forward to lively discussion.

7:00 pm - 8:45 pm Tony Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Anthony Bourdain's creative origins come to life in this coming-of-age biopic starring Dominic Sessa and Antonio Banderas.

In 1975, 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain (Dominic Sessa) wants to be a writer, but instead takes a summer job at a Cape Cod restaurant. Under the tutelage of a Brazilian-born restaurateur (Antonio Banderas), Bourdain stumbles into the chaotic world of the restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life and career.

Director Matt Johnson (BlackBerry) trades the full circumference biopic for a sharper, single slice of Anthony Bourdain's life. An origin story with a few charming poetic liberties (that Bourdain himself would probably "okay"), Tony is equal parts sweet and tart, a splendid tribute to mentorship, and a glimpse at the experiences that would soon make him a beloved culinary figure.

4:00 pm - 5:15 pm Underland (with writer Robert Macfarlane in person) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Based on Robert Macfarlane's bestseller, this hypnotic documentary follows three "astronauts of the underworld" on their journey below the surface of the earth.

Beginning in the shallow soil beneath an ancient ash tree, we travel into sacred ancient caves, flooded storm drains and deep underground laboratories designed to unravel the universe's mysteries. Narrated by Sandra Hüller with poetic sensitivity, the film presents a groundbreaking perspective on our relationship with the earth beneath our feet—a realm that most associate only with darkness and fear but that holds wonder and knowledge for those courageous enough to explore. 

Produced by Darren Aronofsky, Underland offers a rare documentary experience that serves simultaneously as visual splendor, an environmental statement and a philosophical inquiry. This film challenges perceptions and expands understanding of our planet's hidden dimensions, delivering beauty, science and wonder in equal measure, resulting in a profound reevaluation of the ground beneath our feet.

Discussion follows with writer Robert Macfarlane

Co-sponsored by the Department of Environmental Studies and the Department of Anthropology. Please also join us for Robert Macfarlane's writer's talk on Oct 5 in Top of the Hop.

5 pm - 6 pm Lecture on Inequality, Discrimination, and Opportunity Location TBD

The Department of Economics is pleased to sponsor this lecture series to deepen Dartmouth students' understanding of the role of inequality, discrimination, and opportunity in society and to highlight how economics can increase our understanding of these phenomena and inform policy responses.

Regularization and Development. A Decade of Evidence from Colombia

Abstract:
Colombia stands as a pioneer in refugee policy. By granting a regularization status to more than two million Venezuelans, it has showcased the potential of a self-inclusion model in which refugees can work, move freely, and access public services as any other vulnerable population. This lecture summarizes a decade of research on what that model has meant for the economic, social, and political structures of host communities, and for the lives of migrants themselves, in both the short and the long run. It closes with two new studies, one tracing the medium run effects of regularization on migrant social capital, the other its public health externalities.

Sandra V. Rozo is a Senior Economist in the Development Research Group at the World Bank, Faculty Affiliate at UC Berkeley’s CEGA and EGAP, Research Fellow at IZA, and Associate Editor of the Journal of Development Economics. Her research examines how forced displacement affects development and how we can support displaced populations and their hosting communities effectively. She co-founded major studies on forced migration, including VenRePs and the Syrian Refugee Life Study, and contributed to the World Development Report 2023. She is the recipient of the 2024 Juan Luis Londoño Award, awarded biennially to Colombians under 40 whose work has significantly improved welfare in Colombia. Her work spans Latin America, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Africa, including multiple randomized control trials.

Co-Sponsored with:  Sadie Alexander Association

The Department of History welcomes guest scholar A. K. Sandoval-Strausz (Professor of History at Penn State University), to give the annual Robert F. Allabough 1934 Memorial Lecture. Open to all. 

Sandoval-Strausz was born in New York City to immigrant parents. He teaches courses in Latino studies, urban history, spatial theory, sociability, and immigration. His books have won multiple international history awards: Hotel: An American History (Yale University Press, 2007) and Barrio America: How Latino Immigrants Saved the American City (Basic Books, 2019). From the Elwha to the Klamath: on the lives, deaths and rights of rivers

A contemporary de-damming movement is sweeping Europe and the United States. Last year 542 dams were removed across 23 European countries, and 100 dams came down across 30 US states, reconnecting 4900 miles of waterway: more than in any previous year in history. New Hampshire is part of this shift, with dams coming down on the Cocheco, the Piscataquog and the Merrimack, among others. The de-damming movement has accelerated in tandem with, and often in partnership with, the Rights of Nature movement, which argues for a categorical shift in perception and treatment (legal, structural and cultural-imaginative) of ecosystems from resource to relative, object to fellow subject and use value to intrinsic value –– and proposes recognizing rivers always-already as the bearers of fundamental rights.

This 2026 George Link Jr Environmental Awareness Lecture by the British writer Robert Macfarlane will explore what flows from the recognition of rivers as having lives, deaths and rights. By means of story and reportage as well as history, it will traces some of the complex, contested histories of de-damming and river-rights movements, from the Elwha and Klamath rivers in the Pacific Northwest, the Mutehekau Shipu (Magpie River) in Nitassinan (north-east Québec), the Río Los Cedros in Ecuador, and the resurgent 'river-guardianship' movement in England. It will also argue for the vital roles of storytelling, music and art (or what Arne Naess called 'beautiful acts') in inspiring river-activism and, by extension, wider global currents of change.

This event is sponsored by the Hopkins Center for the Arts at Dartmouth, the Department of Environmental Studies, and the Department of Anthropology.

12:15 pm - 1:00 pm Research Talk with Professor of Geography Justin Mankin 0102 Gallery, Visual Arts Center

Mankin's research on climate variability and change is motivated by the risks global warming poses to ecosystems and people. Using observations alongside empirical and process-based models, his efforts are prospective—focused constraining uncertainties in future climate impacts—and retrospective—attributing the climate impacts that have already occured. He is committed to ensuring that climate data are a public good and his hope is that his science can help inform climate adaptation and decision-making. In his previous career, Dr. Mankin worked overseas as an intelligence officer.

Set in rural Vermont, The Neighbors is a multimedia video installation about the non-human inhabitants of the lands around the artist’s home. After over two decades living in San Francisco, California, Sollars moved to Vermont in the fall of 2024. To get to know his new home and neighbors, he has spent the past two years interacting with his surroundings through slow listening and observation, learning them spatially and temporally.  This intentional gathering of information has taken the form of diaristic snapshots taken throughout the seasons, field recordings, the collection of discarded nests and materials, and the placement of wildlife cameras in the open woodland edges of his home, which neighbors a land trust, a national forest, and the Appalachian Trail.

The Neighbors is on view from Sept. 15 – Nov. 8, 2026.

5:00pm Meet Lucy Stone: Enter the Antebellum World of the Abolition and Women's Rights Movements Gay Kimball Library 10 South Main Street Troy New Hampshire 03465

In this first-person interpretive program, Judith Black introduces American Lucy Stone, the first woman hired by the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society as a public speaker and the "Shining Star" of the Abolition and Women's Rights Movements. The presenter dispels well-worn platitudes about the antebellum North by interjecting historic and personal truths about these social reform movements. Her presentation also paints a dynamic and detailed picture of what it takes to change the world you are born into. Follow Lucy as she makes her case for tax resistance, her challenges to marriage laws and motherhood, and her pro-Emancipation response to the Civil War. Go with her to The American Equal Rights Association Convention in May 1869, where she eloquently supports the 15th Amendment, which gave African-American men the vote. 

This is an in person event. We will provide refreshments. This event is open to the public.

6:00pm The Connecticut: New England's Great River Claremont Claremont NH 03743

The largest river in New England rises in a small beaver pond near the Canadian border and flows over 400 miles through four states, falling 2,670 feet to the sea through America's only watershed-based national fish and wildlife refuge. Adair Mulligan leads an armchair tour of this great river in New Hampshire and Vermont, exploring its history and natural beauty through the seasons and among the communities that have sprung up along its banks. Next, the discussion will shift to how the river has influenced the lives of those who live there, and how they, in turn, have affected the river. Much more than a travelogue, this presentation explores the many issues involved in managing the health of this major river, and how citizens from all walks of life have created a vision for its future.

New Hampshire was once home to over 300 covered bridges. Today, there are over sixty authentic covered bridges in New Hampshire, forty-six of which are over a century old. These bridges exist solely because of the efforts of a small but powerful community that both recognized their significance and honored their tradition. Join author and photographer Kim Varney Chandler as she shares an overview of covered bridges in the Granite State, along with interesting facts she uncovered while researching her 2022 book, Covered Bridges of New Hampshire. Learn more about both existing and lost covered bridges in your area.

6:30pm Brewing in New Hampshire: An Informal History of Beer in the Granite State Oscar Foss Memorial Library 111 South Barnstead Road Barnstead NH 03225

Glenn Knoblock explores the fascinating history of New Hampshire's beer and ale brewing industry from Colonial days, when it was home- and tavern-based, to today's modern breweries and brew pubs. Unusual and rare photos and advertisements document this changing industry and the state's earliest brewers, including the renowned Frank Jones. A number of lesser-known brewers and breweries that operated in the state are also discussed, including the only brewery owned and operated by a woman before the modern era. Illustrations present evidence of society's changing attitudes towards beer and alcohol consumption over the years. Whether you're a beer connoisseur or a "tea-totaler", this lecture will be enjoyed by adults of all ages.

7 pm - 9 pm The Alabama Solution Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Inside one of the nation's deadliest prison systems, incarcerated men defy the odds to expose a cover-up in this Oscar-nominated documentary.

In 2019, filmmakers Andrew Jarecki and Charlotte Kaufman visit an Alabama prison to film a revival meeting. Off camera, incarcerated men whisper a message: terrible things are going on here and being kept secret. This sparks an immersive six-year investigation to discover the reality behind the walls of one of the nation's deadliest prison systems.

Composed primarily of contraband cell phone footage taken by incarcerated men at Easterling and other facilities across the state, The Alabama Solution exposes the inhumane conditions, systemic injustice and brutal treatment of those behind bars in the Alabama prison system, told through their own voices and their own stories. The film expertly weaves the pressing issues of prison privatization, inmate slave labor, abuse of power, government corruption and extreme violence together to help audiences on the outside get a real sense of the abhorrent conditions of our fellow human beings. 

Programmed in collaboration with the Dartmouth Prison Justice Initiative. Discussion follows.

 

This event is free but registration is required.

3:30 pm - 4:30 pm High-Throughput Computational Microscopy with Dynamic Samples Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 937 4316 0035
Passcode: 411385

Computational imaging jointly designs hardware and algorithms to push beyond the classical limits of imaging, enabling measurement of new quantities (eg 3D, phase, and super-resolution) with simple, inexpensive hardware. In this talk, I show recent advances that push both spatial and temporal throughput for 2D and 3D fluorescence microscopy. First, I will describe a diffractive, multiplexed microscope that uses engineered point spread functions and a multi-sensor array to achieve gigapixel-scale imaging at video rates, enabling micrometer-resolution imaging over centimeter-scale fields of view for dynamic biological systems. Second, I will introduce a neural space-time model that jointly reconstructs images and motion from sequential measurements, eliminating motion artifacts while recovering sample dynamics without training data or priors. Together, these approaches illustrate a shift from static imaging toward high-throughput, dynamic measurement, opening new opportunities for observing complex biological processes across scales.

Hosted by Professor Irene Georgakoudi

7:00 pm - 9:15 pm El Norte (DFS: Myths Revisited) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Gregory Nava's dramatic 1983 masterpiece weaves in elements of Aztec and Mayan mythology with a quest for the American dream.

After their family is killed in a union-busting government massacre, indigenous Mayan siblings Enrique and Rosa decide to flee Guatemala and embark on a perilous journey to America— "El Norte"—in search of a better life. Facing danger and persecution on every step of the way, their love and resolve eventually bring them to shimmery Los Angeles, which soon proves to be gilded rather than gold.

A tour de force of independent filmmaking, Pava expertly weaves Aztec and Mayan mythology with the modern American Dream, blending magical realism with poignant social commentary as he captures the realities of the modern immigrant experience.

Programmed in collaboration with Professor Gerd Gemunden's class on Migration Stories

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited"

7:30 pm - 8:30 pm Noli Timere Moore Theater, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Witness a gravity-defying world that challenges us to "be not afraid."

Director & Choreographer: Rebecca Lazier
Visual Artist: Janet Echelman
Composer: Jorane

A vast web sets the stage for a breathtaking aerial experience that reflects the interdependence among humans and our environment. Conceived by Guggenheim Fellowship Award-winning choreographer Rebecca Lazier and large-scale fiber artist Janet Echelman, Noli Timere dissolves the boundary between choreography and sculpture, creating a shared system in which body and environment continuously transform one another. With original music by acclaimed Québécois composer Jorane, the mesmerizing work explores how we navigate an unstable world.

Noli Timere is made possible with the generous support of the New England Foundation for the Arts' National Dance Project, with lead funding from the Doris Duke Foundation and The Mellon Foundation; Canada's National Arts Centre's National Creation Fund, Guggenheim Foundation, Innovation Fund for Research Collaborations between Artists and Scientists or Engineers at Princeton University, Canada Council for The Arts, Arts Nova Scotia; Nova Scotia Department of Communities, Culture and Heritage, City of Halifax.

Noli Timere benefited from multiple residencies, including a four-week residency at PS21 Center for Contemporary Performance in Chatham, NY; the Princeton University Atelier Program; the Barrry Onouye Studio at the University of Washington Architecture Department; and at Breaking Circus (Halifax, Nova Scotia), Mocean Dance (Halifax, Nova Scotia) and Universcene (Montreal). Live Art Dance, Princeton University and Mocean Dance commissioned Noli Timere.

Why are we so fascinated with stone walls? Kevin Gardner, author of The Granite Kiss, explains how and why New England came to acquire its thousands of miles of stone walls, the ways that they and other dry stone structures were built, how their styles emerged and changed over time, and their significance to the famous New England landscape. 10:00am The History of Agriculture as Told by Barns Greenfield Historical society 828 Forest Road Greenfield, NH NH 03047

Barns can tell us a great deal about the history of agriculture in New Hampshire. In the colonial period, New Hampshire was a rural, agrarian state and small subsistence farms dotted the landscape. An important part of these farmsteads was the barn, which housed animals and stored crops. Early barns used traditional building methods and followed the English barn style, with a low pitched roof and doors under the eaves. As time went on, the farms expanded to accommodate changes in agriculture. This presentation will follow the progression of barn styles that evolved to handle the increased productivity required to meet the needs of a growing population and respond to changes in society caused by the railroad and the Industrial Revolution. John C. Porter, author of Preserving Old Barns: Preventing the Loss of a Valuable Resource, will demonstrate how these majestic barn structures represent Yankee ingenuity, hard work, and skilled craftsmanship, as well as providing a link to our past that adds to the state's scenic beauty. 

This will be an in-person program with a light lunch available. This program is being coordinated with the dedication of our new barn/carriage shed, honoring a fine former Greenfield resident, Carl Inglestrom, who spent his career in the field of agriculture. The venue will be at least partially outside, weather permitting.

1 pm - 3 pm 107 Days at Sea: The Journey That Changed Everything Auditorium E, Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center One Medical Center Drive, Lebanon, NH 03766

At 63, Jill Chalsty boarded a ship alone, grieving her husband’s death and battling cancer. What began as a voyage around the world became far more than a trip. In this lecture, Jill shares the story behind her memoir Packets of Hope, inviting participants to travel alongside her through the ports she visited, the people she met, and the reflections that transformed personal adversity into strength and global impact. Jill demonstrates how one person’s courage can create ripples that span continents.

Participants are encouraged to read her memoir, available free at www.packetsofhope.com, before the presentation.

Jill Siegal Chalsty has devoted her life to the transformative power of education. As founder of Overcoming Obstacles, the nonprofit she launched in 1992, Jill pioneered life skills instruction that has now reached more than 180 million students worldwide. What began as a mission to help young people navigate life’s challenges has evolved into a global movement for youth empowerment. Following the profound loss of her husband and her own battles with cancer, Jill embarked on a voyage of healing and reflection. That journey inspired her memoir, Packets of Hope, an exploration of resilience, love, and finding meaning through service. She's made her book available for free at packetsofhope.com.

7:00 pm - 9:30 pm National Theatre in HD: The Misanthrope Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Sandra Oh stars in this razor-sharp reimagining of Molière's classic dark comedy.

Alice (Sandra Oh), a brilliant novelist, despises the hollow contemporary mantras of kindness and respect. But the bolder she becomes in speaking out, the more colleagues avoid her, and the more her personal relationships begin to fracture. As she challenges fashionable ideas and lends her voice to causes others are afraid to touch, she faces intense criticism and backlash. Alice will soon learn the price she must pay as an artist and as a woman for daring to speak her mind.  

First performed on 15 June 1666 at the Théâtre du Palais‑Royal in Paris, The Misanthrope emerged at a pivotal moment in the reign of Louis XIV, when court life, power and social conventions weighed heavily on the public conscience. In this context, Molière crafted a verse comedy as serious as it is brilliant, questioning the role of sincerity in a world ruled by appearances. Less farcical than his other plays, it stands as a masterpiece of balance between social satire and emotional tension—and this new production shows these moral dilemmas are utterly timeless.

7:00pm Brewing in New Hampshire: An Informal History of Beer in the Granite State Gafney Library 14 High Street Sanbornville New Hampshire 03872

Glenn Knoblock explores the fascinating history of New Hampshire's beer and ale brewing industry from Colonial days, when it was home- and tavern-based, to today's modern breweries and brew pubs. Unusual and rare photos and advertisements document this changing industry and the state's earliest brewers, including the renowned Frank Jones. A number of lesser-known brewers and breweries that operated in the state are also discussed, including the only brewery owned and operated by a woman before the modern era. Illustrations present evidence of society's changing attitudes towards beer and alcohol consumption over the years. Whether you're a beer connoisseur or a "tea-totaler", this lecture will be enjoyed by adults of all ages.

This program will be held in the Community Room of the Gafney Library, located on the lower level. There is an elevator and stairs available. Free parking is across the street. No registration is required and there will be a social time after the program with snacks.

8:30 pm - 11:00 pm Metropolis (DFS: Myths Revisited) Rollins Chapel

Fritz Lang's crown jewel of silent cinema fuses the frenetic storytelling of 1920s pulp fiction with his fascination with the darker side of human nature.

Set in the year 2026, society has been divided into two rigid groups: one of rich planners or thinkers, who live in luxury on the surface of Earth in the lush skyscrapers; the other of workers, who live underground, toiling to sustain the lives of the privileged up above. Both halves are ignorant of each other. It is only when Freder Fredersen, the son of the rich city master, meets the saintly Maria from below, that he descends and sees the lives and machines that keep his society afloat. 

Determined to be the "Mediator" that Maria prophesizes to the workers, Freder must fight against lies and deception to unite the "head" of his world with the "hands" down below. Full of Biblical references and religious allegory, Metropolis fixed for the rest of the century the image of a futuristic city as a hell of scientific progress and human despair, and inspired countless narratives from Star Wars to Blade Runner. 

With live organ accompaniment by Peter Krasinski

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited." Programmed in collaboration with the William Jewett Tucker Center for Spiritual, the Department of Film & Media Studies and Ethical Living, the Church of Christ at Dartmouth College

 

This event is free and unticketed.

6:00pm Corbin’s Animal Garden Walpole Town Library 48 Main Street Walpole NH 03608

In the late 1800s, the banking, railroad, and real estate mogul Austin Corbin returned to his hometown in Newport, New Hampshire. He built a grand estate and bought out his neighbors’ farms to create an 22,000 acre wildlife game preserve stocked with boar, bison, bighorn sheep, antelope, elk, Chinese pheasant, and other imported animals. The grounds eventually became a prestigious private hunting park and hosted illustrious guests including Theodore Roosevelt, the Prince of Wales, Cornelius Vanderbilt, Joe DiMaggio, Rudyard Kipling, and Augustus Saint-Gaudens.

This illustrated slideshow features archival images and a discussion of the complicated history and legacy of New Hampshire’s own American Gilded Age robber baron. The talk will also highlight the important legacy of the role the Corbin family and park naturalist Ernest Baynes played in the saving of the American bison from extinction.

Pre-registration is recommended. To register, call 603-756-9806 or email  jmalmberg@walpoletownlibrary.org.

Thursday, October 15
Dartmouth 105

Free & Open to All

Elizabeth Greene, University of Western Ontario

Talk title: Archaeological Leather and the Precarious Future of Organic Material Evidence

Abstract: The Roman site of Vindolanda on the northern frontier of Britain has provided one of the best assemblages of organic material from anywhere in the empire. Over eight thousand leather finds, including nearly five thousand shoes, and countless wood and bone objects, have provided a more complete picture of life in the past than is typical of most sites. However, this invaluable resource is also under threat from environmental shifts, and Vindolanda is leading the way on several initiatives to understand how climate change is affecting archaeological remains. This talk will first present current work on archaeological leather and then focus on its role in assessing the impact of climate change on archaeology and organic artifacts.

Generously funded by Gino Franco Luigi Zarbin, MD Memorial Fund in Classics.

4:30 pm - 6:30 pm Saints and Silks: The global reach of Latin Christianity in the Middle Ages Carson Hall L02

Julia Smith, Emeritus Chichele Professor of Medieval History, All Souls College
Oxford University

Thursday, October 15, 2026
4:30 PM
Location: Carson L02 (tentative)
Free and open to all

Reception to follow

Lecture title: Saints and Silks: The global reach of Latin Christianity in the early Middle Ages

Abstract: This illustrated lecture uses the contents of Christian reliquaries from the first half of the European Middle Ages to reflect on how relics accumulated in medieval churches and how their textile wrappers enhanced their sacred aura.  In so doing, it offers a focussed way of thinking through some of the implications of the global turn for study of medieval Europe.  Utilising textual sources such as relic labels and inventories on the one hand and, on the other, material evidence, especially textiles, it takes an ‘object biography’ approach to emphasise the rich complexity of ecclesiastical relic collections.  While the examples chosen will span Eurasia, the argument emphasises the local contexts in which relics accumulated and thus the distinctive profile of each collection.  The lecture replaces conventional textbook accounts of the early medieval West with a dynamic picture of contingency, mobility, and repurposing which sustained the religious capital of early medieval churches in the Latin West.

The James and David Orr Memorial Lectures on Culture and Religion bring to Dartmouth each year scholars and writers whose achievements are at the highest level, but whose main fields of interest are not necessarily religion. Past Orr Lecturers include historians, anthropologists, novelists, biologists, and philosophers.

5 pm - 6 pm The Eclecticism of Moderation with Aurelian Craiutu, Indiana University Room 002, Rockefeller Center

Moderation is a contested concept that, with surprisingly few exceptions, is absent from our public debates. Today, the single famous line that people sometimes may remember belongs to Barry Goldwater: “Extremism in the pursuit of liberty is no vice, moderation in the pursuit of justice is no virtue.” His witty words continue to provoke and invite us to rethink the nature of moderation and examine its eclecticism. The latter can be explored by looking at the many faces of moderation and the various agendas and principles moderates of all types advanced over time. 

The lecture will address the following questions: What kind of virtue is political moderation and how can we study it? What does it mean to be a moderate voice in politics? What are the limits and benefits of moderation? Finally, can moderation be a winning card in our hyper-polarized political world?

Craiutu is the Arthur F. Bentley Professor and Chair of the Department of Political Science at Indiana University, Bloomington. His most recent book is Why Not Moderation? Letters to a Young Radical (Cambridge University Press, 2024). His talk is sponsored by the Political Economy Project and the Rockefeller Center.

6:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution Kimball Library 5 Academy Avenue Atkinson NH 03811

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

7:00 pm - 8:15 pm Preconceived Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

A riveting documentary about the pervasive but overlooked presence of Crisis Pregnancy Centers.

Where does someone turn when facing an unplanned pregnancy? This even-handed film offers a raw and insightful look into the rise of the enigmatic crisis pregnancy centers (CPCs), many of which are a part of a movement striving to make abortion unthinkable and illegal. The documentary explores the complex role of deception, finances, faith and privacy in the CPC industry, while also showing that many of the people involved genuinely believe they are serving the greater good.

Preconceived follows the stories of two women, Maleeha in Texas and Maria in Colorado, whose searches to terminate their unplanned pregnancies misled them to anti-abortion centers. The film also features testimonies from individuals on both sides of the issue, including leaders of the CPC industry as well as experts who caution why many CPC practices are problematic. Amid a shifting legal landscape, Preconceived deftly navigates the complicated political and moral knot that is abortion access in America and underscores the importance of understanding the resources available to pregnant people.

Discussion follows. Co-hosted by the Dartmouth Democrats and the Hanover/Lyme Democrats, in collaboration with Reproductive Equity Now.

This event is free but registration is required.

5 pm - 6 pm The Everywhere Millionaire with Professor Owen Zidar '08, Princeton University Room 003, Rockefeller Center

A professor of economics and public policy at Princeton University, Zidar (Class of '08) will discuss his just-published, ground-breaking book. Drawing on unprecedented data from a decade of research and vivid real-life stories of entrepreneurs―from a self-made hot-dog stand billionaire to the heirs of an auto dealer―Zidar and co-author Erich Zwick reveal a surprising truth: prosperity is more attainable, more widely distributed, and closer to home than we imagine. A multitude of Americans have built staggering fortunes by running often unglamorous businesses far from the spotlight. A quiet revolution in the business world―the rise of “pass-through” firms like S-corporations and partnerships―supercharged this wealth, channeling vast income directly to business owners rather than traditional corporations. Sponsored by the Political Economy Project and co-sponsored by the Rockefeller Center.

Political Economy Project, Rockefeller Center

7:00 pm - 7:30 pm Forgotten Founder Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

This new documentary uncovers the history of Mohegan minister and educator Samson Occom, whose fundraising efforts were instrumental in Dartmouth's founding.

Co-directed by Melissa Tantaquidgeon Zobel, a direct descendant of Occom, and filmmaker Signe Taylor, this new documentary uncovers the largely erased history of Samson Occom, a Mohegan minister, educator and Indigenous intellectual whose fundraising efforts were instrumental in the founding of Dartmouth College. Despite his central role, Occom's contributions—and the promises made to Native communities—were minimized or omitted from the historical record.

Weaving together past and present through an intimate, intergenerational lens, the film features three of Occom's descendants—two as interview participants and one portraying Occom on screen—creating a rare dialogue between history, memory and lived experience. Through Indigenous voices, archival materials and embodied performance, Forgotten Founder explores legacy, accountability and survival.

The preeminent pipa virtuoso brings ancient Chinese tradition to today's global stage. Wu Man shares this bespoke program while in residence as a principal collaborator of Kronos Quartet.

Experience the artistry of the world's foremost player of the pipa in a solo setting. Wu Man is a composer, educator and virtuosic performer of the traditional Chinese lute with equal respect for preservation and innovation. 

A champion of new music and cross-cultural collaboration, she has premiered hundreds of new works for her instrument in settings from solo recitals to collaborations with the New York Philharmonic, Boston Symphony Orchestra, Yo-Yo Ma, Kronos Quartet and Silkroad Ensemble.

Wu Man's repertoire, heard in the world's foremost venues and on Grammy Award-winning recordings, spans traditional Chinese music, cross-cultural fusion and contemporary works by today's leading composers.

Use abstract thinking to create illustrative paintings

Aline Ordman is an experienced teacher and artist, well known for her vivid paintings and creative use of color. Painting is learning to see, and Aline teaches students to see differently. Rather than painting preconceived notions of what something looks like, she guides them to break down the visual world into abstract shapes. Not a "house," but a series of interlocking forms.

Working from their own photo references, students will transform images into pastel paintings using the principles of color and design. Drum Building Workshop

Build Your Own 13″ Sacred Deer Medicine Drum

Saturday, October 17, 2026
10:00 AM – 5:00 PM

$295 Appreciation Exchange

The drum is one of humanity’s oldest and most sacred instruments. Its steady rhythm mirrors the heartbeat of Mother Earth and our own heartbeat, connecting us to the natural world and to ancient traditions that have honored the drum for thousands of years. Used for meditation, ceremony, healing, and celebration, the drum invites us to slow down, listen deeply, and reconnect with ourselves.

Join Master Drumsmith Jane E. King for a meaningful, hands-on workshop where you will create your own 13-inch Sacred Deer Medicine Drum from natural materials. Throughout the day, Jane will guide you through each step of the drum-making process while honoring the spirit of the deer, the gifts of the natural world, and your own personal intentions.

The sacred process of birthing your own personal deer medicine drum is much more than a craft—it is an opportunity for self-discovery, mindfulness, and spiritual connection. As you work with the deer hide, wooden hoop, and the elements of water, air, earth, and fire, you will create an instrument that reflects your own energy, purpose, and healing journey.

Your workshop experience begins with a guided inward journey to connect with the spirit of Deer and receive personal messages and teachings. From there, you will prayerfully prepare and lace your drum, infusing it with intention, gratitude, and your own unique medicine. Whether you are experienced in spiritual practices or completely new to drum making, Jane’s gentle instruction creates a welcoming and supportive environment for everyone.

You will also create a matching drum beater (drumstick), completing a beautiful and functional instrument that you can continue to use for meditation, ceremony, music, healing work, or personal reflection for years to come.

Workshop Includes:

  • A handcrafted 13″ Sacred Deer Medicine Drum
  • A matching handmade drum beater
  • All natural materials and supplies
  • Step-by-step instruction by Master Drumsmith Jane E. King
  • Guided meditation and spiritual journey
  • A full day of creativity, reflection, and community

No previous experience is necessary. All materials and instruction are included.

Whether you feel called to deepen your spiritual practice, honor nature through traditional craftsmanship, or simply experience the joy of creating something meaningful with your own hands, this workshop offers a unique opportunity to craft an instrument that will carry your intentions long after the day is over.

Space is limited, and early registration is encouraged.

1:00 pm - 1:30 pm Forgotten Founder Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

This new documentary uncovers the history of Mohegan minister and educator Samson Occom, whose fundraising efforts were instrumental in Dartmouth's founding.

Co-directed by Melissa Tantaquidgeon Zobel, a direct descendant of Occom, and filmmaker Signe Taylor, this new documentary uncovers the largely erased history of Samson Occom, a Mohegan minister, educator and Indigenous intellectual whose fundraising efforts were instrumental in the founding of Dartmouth College. Despite his central role, Occom's contributions—and the promises made to Native communities—were minimized or omitted from the historical record.

Weaving together past and present through an intimate, intergenerational lens, the film features three of Occom's descendants—two as interview participants and one portraying Occom on screen—creating a rare dialogue between history, memory and lived experience. Through Indigenous voices, archival materials and embodied performance, Forgotten Founder explores legacy, accountability and survival.

Discussion follows.

Oct 17 – Oct 18, 2026 Oval Box Making Workshop Enfield Shaker Museum

$265 – $285

Shaker Oval Box Making Workshop

Saturday, October 17 and Sunday, October 18, 2026

8:30 am – 4:00 pm

Learn how to make your own nest of Shaker oval boxes in our Shaker Oval Box Making Workshop. Guided by experienced box maker John Cashman, you will make five (5) Shaker Oval Nesting Boxes, from Pennsylvania cherry wood. The class will focus on preparing the wood, cutting swallowtail fingers, bending the sides and rims, and applying a finish. These iconic Shaker oval boxes are made with copper tacks and wooden pegs using the same techniques practiced by the Shaker brothers in their workshops.

No previous woodworking experience necessary. Beginners are welcome!

Students who have completed the basic class are welcome back to build an assortment of larger boxes, trays, and carriers.

All tools and materials supplied. Students can bring their own eye and ear protection and dust masks, but we will have enough on hand for everyone. We will break for an hour each day for lunch. There are a couple of meal options nearby, but they are limited. Consider bringing a bag lunch and water/beverage.

Museum Member – $265/person

Non-Member – $285/person

Materials Fee – $25/per person, paid directly to the instructor

Class size is limited to 12. Advance registration is required.

All proceeds from this workshop go to support the educational mission of Enfield Shaker Museum.

Coming from a distance? Why not plan to stay overnight in the historic Great Stone Dwelling? Check out room availability here.

Want to know more about John Cashman?

John Cashman has been making oval boxes for over 15 years. He’s been an avid student of box making, studying both original Shaker-made boxes and modern production methods. He’s made boxes as small as a quarter, and as large as a coffee table. John sells his boxes through the Shaker museum shops at Enfield, NH and Sabbathday Lake, Maine. He’s recently had a nest of 15 boxes exhibited at The Fuller Craft Museum.
